Committee of Origin: Health & Human Services
Re: Regulating the Use of Plastics in Food Preparation & Storage in New York State.
Full Board Vote: 36 In Favor 1 Against 2 Abstentions 0 Present
The following facts and concerns were taken into consideration:
Plastic chemicals having endocrine disrupting activity (ED) are reported to cause many adverse
health effects, including cancers, birth defects, impaired immunity, endocrine disruption, hormone
imbalances, and developmental and reproductive effects, particularly among fetal and juvenile mammals.
95% of commercially available plastic products have been found to leach chemicals with reliably
detectable ED, particularly when exposed to sunlight, microwaving, dishwashing, and other heating
(including those advertised as BPA, PVC and Phthalate-free, among others), which can increase the rate of
leaching up to 55 times.
Such chemicals can be found in tap water, food packaging, cosmetics (e.g. shampoo, nail polish,
hair spray, and perfumes), vinyl flooring, detergent, clothing, shower curtains, furniture, cars, rain, and
stain-resistant products, among others.
Bisphenol (BPA), phthalates, alkylphenols, polyvinyl chloride PFAS and other chemicals have been
studied extensively, so manufacturers are switching to lesser-known plastic additives with unknown risks
and marketing such products as “BPA-free” (among other names), while replacement additives such as
BPA S have proven to be similarly hazardous to human health.
Detectable levels of bisphenol A (BPA) and phthalates from plastics have been found in the urine
of 95% of adults in the United States, rendering it difficult to create a control group for scientific
comparison.
Petrochemical products, containing plastics represent a $439 billion dollar industry in the United
States as of 2021, amount to 14% of oil- consumption, and it is estimated that they will account for up to
half of oil demand growth between now and 2050.
Sperm count declines in the West of 59% between 1973 and 2011 are thought to be attributable
to phthalates found in plastics, among other causes.
In July 2012 the FDA amended its regulations to disallow the use of BPA in baby bottles, sippy cups,
and formula packaging due to concerns over its link to developmental delays. Plastic chemicals were
linked to $249 billion in health care costs in the United States in 2018.
Children are at greater risk from small quantities of chemicals than adults: the National Cancer
Institute estimates that there has been a 27% increase in the overall rate of childhood cancers since 1975,
and links to neurodevelopmental harm, early onset puberty, and other health issues are well
documented.
Food and beverages account for most of the daily human exposure to such chemicals.
Assemblymember Linda Rosenthal has proposed legislation to regulate the use of plastics, as follows:
• A3424 - This legislation would prohibit food service establishments from providing single-use
plastic utensils, condiment packets and other items unless requested by the customer.
Additionally, it would prohibit establishments statewide from using single-use plastic straws,
requiring that eateries use an alternative.
• A8826 - This legislation would expand on a current state regulation that prohibits state agencies
from purchasing single-use plastic water bottles. The bill expands it to all plastic beverage bottles.

year. West Prep is a district middle school serving students in grades 6-8 in M145, located at 150 West
105th Street (between Amsterdam and Columbus Ave.). It is currently co-located with P.S. 145, The
Bloomingdale School (03M145), a district elementary school serving students in 3K - grade 5. The NYCDOE

Building M534 is located at 220 West 108th Street (between Broadway and Amsterdam Avenues),
approximately 0.3 miles from M145 and has been acquired by the School Construction Authority (SCA)
and NYCDOE M534. The NYCDOE says the M534 building is expected to be ready for occupancy prior to
the start of the 2024-2025 school year.

Date: March 5, 2024
Committee of Origin: Health & Human Services
Re: Regulating the Use of Plastics in Food Preparation & Storage in New York State.
Full Board Vote: 36 In Favor 1 Against 2 Abstentions 0 Present
The following facts and concerns were taken into consideration:
Plastic chemicals having endocrine disrupting activity (ED) are reported to cause many adverse
health effects, including cancers, birth defects, impaired immunity, endocrine disruption, hormone
imbalances, and developmental and reproductive effects, particularly among fetal and juvenile mammals.
95% of commercially available plastic products have been found to leach chemicals with reliably
detectable ED, particularly when exposed to sunlight, microwaving, dishwashing, and other heating
(including those advertised as BPA, PVC and Phthalate-free, among others), which can increase the rate of
leaching up to 55 times.
Such chemicals can be found in tap water, food packaging, cosmetics (e.g. shampoo, nail polish,
hair spray, and perfumes), vinyl flooring, detergent, clothing, shower curtains, furniture, cars, rain, and
stain-resistant products, among others.
Bisphenol (BPA), phthalates, alkylphenols, polyvinyl chloride PFAS and other chemicals have been
studied extensively, so manufacturers are switching to lesser-known plastic additives with unknown risks
and marketing such products as “BPA-free” (among other names), while replacement additives such as
BPA S have proven to be similarly hazardous to human health.
Detectable levels of bisphenol A (BPA) and phthalates from plastics have been found in the urine
of 95% of adults in the United States, rendering it difficult to create a control group for scientific
comparison.
Petrochemical products, containing plastics represent a $439 billion dollar industry in the United
States as of 2021, amount to 14% of oil- consumption, and it is estimated that they will account for up to
half of oil demand growth between now and 2050.
Sperm count declines in the West of 59% between 1973 and 2011 are thought to be attributable
to phthalates found in plastics, among other causes.
In July 2012 the FDA amended its regulations to disallow the use of BPA in baby bottles, sippy cups,
and formula packaging due to concerns over its link to developmental delays. Plastic chemicals were
linked to $249 billion in health care costs in the United States in 2018.
Children are at greater risk from small quantities of chemicals than adults: the National Cancer
Institute estimates that there has been a 27% increase in the overall rate of childhood cancers since 1975,
and links to neurodevelopmental harm, early onset puberty, and other health issues are well
documented.
Food and beverages account for most of the daily human exposure to such chemicals.
Assemblymember Linda Rosenthal has proposed legislation to regulate the use of plastics, as follows:
• A3424 - This legislation would prohibit food service establishments from providing single-use
plastic utensils, condiment packets and other items unless requested by the customer.
Additionally, it would prohibit establishments statewide from using single-use plastic straws,
requiring that eateries use an alternative.
• A8826 - This legislation would expand on a current state regulation that prohibits state agencies
from purchasing single-use plastic water bottles. The bill expands it to all plastic beverage bottles.

Full Board Vote: 37 In Favor 0 Against 1 Abstention 0 Present
Committee: 10-0-1-0. Non-Committee Board Members: 1-0-0-0.
This resolution is based on the following facts:
• “Daylighting” is the practice of reserving a defined space at adjacent intersections on streets and
avenues to remain free of parking and other obstructions to ensure that pedestrians can see
oncoming vehicles of all types, and that the oncoming vehicles can see pedestrians.
• CB7 adopted a resolution on November 4, 2020 calling for Daylighting at all intersections within a
one-block radius of any school, senior center or facility for the disabled.
• The NYC Department of Transportation confirmed to CB7 on March 30, 2022, that “Daylighting can
be a valuable tool for improving visibility at certain intersections, particularly intersections without
signals and with specific geometric conditions that affect visibility,” but cautioned that Daylighting
“could inadvertently allow vehicles to turn faster by widening the roadway on the approach” and
could be used by delivery vehicles, “which can negatively impact visibility.”
• Including lo-scale obstructions such as planters, boulders, solid curb extensions and other objects
are effective means to prevent unauthorized use of the reserved space and shorten the turning
radius and require vehicles to slow down before turning.
• While prioritizing our most mobility-challenged residents is appropriate, CB7 believes that
pedestrian safety issues should be universally applied except where such measures interfere with
other safety concerns.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan calls on DoT:
A. to implement Daylighting at all Upper West Side intersections where DoT determines it
to be safe and feasible, using the tools in its toolbox including without limitation planters,
boulders, and solid curb extensions, to prevent both faster turning and unauthorized use
of the reserved space;
B. timely report to MCB7 any intersections at which competing safety concerns lead DoT to
recommend not implementing Daylighting at that specific location; and
C. to prioritize Daylighting at the following locations:

(03M421) from building M145 to building M534 (formerly the Ascension School) in the 2024-2025 school
year. West Prep is a district middle school serving students in grades 6-8 in M145, located at 150 West
105th Street (between Amsterdam and Columbus Ave.). It is currently co-located with P.S. 145, The
Bloomingdale School (03M145), a district elementary school serving students in 3K - grade 5. The NYCDOE
is proposing this re-siting to address space challenges in the M145 building.
Building M534 is located at 220 West 108th Street (between Broadway and Amsterdam Avenues),
approximately 0.3 miles from M145 and has been acquired by the School Construction Authority (SCA)
and NYCDOE M534. The NYCDOE says the M534 building is expected to be ready for occupancy prior to
the start of the 2024-2025 school year.

and have access to the space they need to serve all their students. Currently the NYCDOE states that West
Prep and P.S. 145 do not have the full complement of instructional, specialty, and/or administrative spaces
which the schools are entitled to base on their current enrollment and programming.

Plastic chemicals having endocrine disrupting activity (ED) are reported to cause many adverse

95% of commercially available plastic products have been found to leach chemicals with reliably

hair spray, and perfumes), vinyl flooring, detergent, clothing, shower curtains, furniture, cars, rain, and
stain-resistant products, among others.

studied extensively, so manufacturers are switching to lesser-known plastic additives with unknown risks
and marketing such products as “BPA-free” (among other names), while replacement additives such as
BPA S have proven to be similarly hazardous to human health.

of 95% of adults in the United States, rendering it difficult to create a control group for scientific
comparison.

States as of 2021, amount to 14% of oil- consumption, and it is estimated that they will account for up to
half of oil demand growth between now and 2050.

to phthalates found in plastics, among other causes.

linked to $249 billion in health care costs in the United States in 2018.

Institute estimates that there has been a 27% increase in the overall rate of childhood cancers since 1975,

documented.

This resolution is based on the following facts:
• “Daylighting” is the practice of reserving a defined space at adjacent intersections on streets and
avenues to remain free of parking and other obstructions to ensure that pedestrians can see
oncoming vehicles of all types, and that the oncoming vehicles can see pedestrians.
• CB7 adopted a resolution on November 4, 2020 calling for Daylighting at all intersections within a
one-block radius of any school, senior center or facility for the disabled.
• The NYC Department of Transportation confirmed to CB7 on March 30, 2022, that “Daylighting can
be a valuable tool for improving visibility at certain intersections, particularly intersections without
signals and with specific geometric conditions that affect visibility,” but cautioned that Daylighting
“could inadvertently allow vehicles to turn faster by widening the roadway on the approach” and
could be used by delivery vehicles, “which can negatively impact visibility.”
• Including lo-scale obstructions such as planters, boulders, solid curb extensions and other objects
are effective means to prevent unauthorized use of the reserved space and shorten the turning
radius and require vehicles to slow down before turning.
• While prioritizing our most mobility-challenged residents is appropriate, CB7 believes that
pedestrian safety issues should be universally applied except where such measures interfere with
other safety concerns.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan calls on DoT:
A. to implement Daylighting at all Upper West Side intersections where DoT determines it
to be safe and feasible, using the tools in its toolbox including without limitation planters,
boulders, and solid curb extensions, to prevent both faster turning and unauthorized use
of the reserved space;
B. timely report to MCB7 any intersections at which competing safety concerns lead DoT to
recommend not implementing Daylighting at that specific location; and
C. to prioritize Daylighting at the following locations:

− West 74th and 75th Streets -- Broadway

Re: DSNY Street Sweeping Plan - Administrative Change to Alternate Side Parking at Riverside Drive
Between 97th and 104th Streets.
Full Board Vote: 36 In Favor 0 Against 0 Abstentions 1 Present
Committee: 5-0-0-0. Non-Committee Board Member: 1-0-0-0.
This resolution is based on the following facts:
• Riverside Drive (Between 97th and 104th streets) has an excess buildup of leaves, trash, and other
debris along the roadway where vehicles park.
• At present, street sweeping is slated to occur two times per-week in the above referenced area
between 11:30AM and 1:30PM.
• Testimony from representatives of nearby block associations, DSNY personnel, and a site visit
conducted by CB7 have confirmed and documented that residents act in good faith and comply
with the requirement to move vehicles during these regularly scheduled windows.
• However, street sweepers too often arrive shortly after this window elapses due to the length of
their current route. As a result, this specific segment of the route does not receive the level of
service needed and remains filled with debris.
• DSNY maintains the ability to change Alternate Side Parking (ASP) and street sweeping
procedures with input from the local community board; and the District 7 Sanitation
Superintendent has shared a willingness to implement changes as needed.
• A change in street sweeping and ASP protocol can improve this level of service.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/ Manhattan proposes and requests the
Department of Sanitation change the plan for street sweeping and ASP on Riverside Drive between 97th
and 104th streets to include dividing the current route and reducing service of each side of said route to
one time per-week in order to satisfactorily clean the streets and remove leaves, trash, and other debris
from them.

between 11:30AM and 1:30PM.

with the requirement to move vehicles during these regularly scheduled windows.

service needed and remains filled with debris.

procedures with input from the local community board; and the District 7 Sanitation
Superintendent has shared a willingness to implement changes as needed.

Department of Sanitation change the plan for street sweeping and ASP on Riverside Drive between 97th
and 104th streets to include dividing the current route and reducing service of each side of said route to
one time per-week in order to satisfactorily clean the streets and remove leaves, trash, and other debris
from them.

suites. Although AC units at lower levels of a building emit noise and hot air is blown outside on the

in each window half, without additional CB7 approval, however, this alternative was unpalatable to the
applicant. There will be no changes to the frame or stone of the window. The color is the one specified in
the master plan for the building and made of the same material as the window frames.

presented, as reasonably appropriate to the building and to the Historic District.

While the 2022 amendment of Open Meetings Law has been a positive development overall, it has
not been perfect. Aspects of the current law have proven extremely challenging for public bodies,
particularly volunteer bodies like Community Education Councils and Community Boards, the latter of
which the Manhattan Borough President’s Office (MBPO) plays a role providing technical support. In
December 2023, the MBPO held a public hearing on Open Meetings Law to collect testimony from New
Yorkers on the benefits, challenges, and suggested amendments to the current law. The response was
overwhelming, with the vast majority of participants asking for additional funding and support, as well as
reductions in the number of individuals required to participate in person.
As currently written, the law requires that each board achieve quorum in-person, which puts
considerable administrative strain on Community Boards, and requires board leadership to make
determinations about who can and cannot participate remotely on their own. While we understand the
importance of having a single location where the public, press and advocates can go to get information or
answers to questions, requiring quorum in-person is an unnecessarily high threshold and risks preventing
boards from being able to conduct business in a timely manner. The current in-person requirement adds
the additional challenge of finding venues that can accommodate the size of quorum plus the public in a
time when such spaces are scarce. This must be and can be easily fixed.
Across the city, we have heard how important and impactful the 2022 amendment to the Open
Meetings Law was. It’s imperative that we further tweak the law to ensure that every public meeting can
be run in a hybrid format successfully, and resource boards to run them effectively. We respectfully urge
the passage of S1647 (Hoylman)/A10276 (Bores).

The following facts and concerns were considered in arriving at our conclusion:
On May 20, 2024, the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation (“DPR”) presented a
comprehensive plan (the “Plan”) for the reconstruction of the Soldiers and Sailors Monument (the
"Monument") located within Riverside Park (the "Park"). The Plan outlines the restoration of the
Monument, including the surrounding terraces and other associated structures. Additionally, it includes
designs for ADA-compliant accessibility on the Monument's exterior levels, as well as possible
improvements to the overall lighting of the structure and the environs.
Located at West 89th Street and Riverside Park Drive, the Monument commemorates Union Army
soldiers and sailors from New York who served in the Civil War. Completed in 1902, it underwent partial
restoration in the 1930s and a full restoration in the 1950s. However, in 2018, due to public safety
concerns, the site was sealed pending repairs. No significant restoration work has been undertaken on
the Monument for over 60 years.
The Plan presented to this committee was partially informed by a 2017 Survey and Restoration
Treatment Study ("2017 Study") conducted by the NYC Office of Management and Budget and DPR.
According to the 2017 Study, the Monument's memorial, ceremonial stairway, and adjacent terraces and
balustrades have experienced significant erosion and decay due to weathering and flooding, and
additional damage from vandals. This study rated the overall condition of the Monument as Fair to Poor.
According to the Plan, while restoration survey work and details are still ongoing, the Plan details
an ADA- accessible design that is still welcoming while minimizing the impact on views of the Monument
or its historical significance. This is accomplished through strategic use of topography, landscaping, and
the creation of switchback paths. Specifically, the Plan proposes expanding the stairs at the upper terrace
and enlarging the landings to connect the paths. It also suggests removing balustrades in two locations to
create landings for these paths and relocating the cannon balls.
The restoration efforts also aim to restore or replace, as needed, the materials of the Monument
structure. This involves restoring or replacing in-kind the existing granite and marble components and
restoring or replacing in-kind the limestone balustrades. The only proposed change in material is the
replacement of the Crab Orchard sandstone, which is in poor condition, with a custom brick design in a
herringbone pattern as per the original design intent. Very importantly, a drainage system shall be
installed for the first time ever at the Monument.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Manhattan Community Board 7 enthusiastically approves the
reconstruction plan of the Soldiers and Sailors Monument as presented. These changes are desperately
needed to remediate issues related to advanced deterioration due to weathering, erosion, and poor
drainage, and also to make the Monument fully ADA-accessible. We request that DPR and other relevant
agencies attend to staging, traffic diversion, and noise issues in a manner that is least disruptive to the
neighborhood and the community once the renovation begins.

This resolution is based on the following information:
• The Department of Parks and Recreation (“DPR”) plans to restore the Sol Bloom Playground (the
“Playground”) located at W. 91st & 92nd St between Columbus Ave & Central Park West
(“Restoration”). The Playground, attached to P.S. 84, the Lillian Weber School (“P.S. 84”), is jointly
operated by DPR and the Department of Education.
• Originally opened in 1962 and last renovated in 1997, the Playground's equipment and safety
surfaces have since become outdated and worn. Further, the Playground lacks accessibility and
experiences drainage issues and occasional flooding. Finally, the Playground lacks tables, updated
water fountains, and a swing set that can accommodate children of all abilities. It should be noted
that the non-ADA compliant public bathroom in the Playground is not within the scope of the
Restoration.
• The goals of the Restoration include upgrading the play structures, increasing accessibility,
providing more spray shower variety, increasing seating and space for children and caregivers,
improving drainage, and optimizing circulation and sight lines. The Restoration plan is based partly
on DPR’s community outreach via Zoom on November 15, 2023, and with 4th graders on site at
P.S. 84. Input was collected from the community and the students on topics like safety, water
play, greenery and seating, among others.
• The Committee finds the design presented by DPR to be imaginative and inclusive, featuring ADA-
accessible and modernized play structures and colorful safety surfaces. The design also includes
new benches, round game tables, additional shade trees, a large spray water feature, and
upgraded water fountains with a water bottle dispenser. Finally, the design added colorful
graphics and reimagined the floorplan, relocating play structures to areas that improved both
accessibility and sight lines.
• The Committee also especially appreciates the project’s focus on sustainability. In this area, the
Restoration seeks to reduce stormwater runoff with rain gardens, use recycled content material,
improve tree health and growing conditions, and use site appropriate resilient plant materials.
These efforts will increase the existing permeability of the site from 0.6% to the proposed
permeability of 5%.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7 / Manhattan approves the restoration
plan for the Sol Bloom Playground, aimed at updating play structures and improving accessibility and
drainage. CB7 appreciates the community outreach conducted in anticipation of this project. Should
additional funds become available, the Board recommends also upgrading the Playground’s bathroom
facilities. We look forward to receiving updates from DPR before construction begins, including detailed
plans for equipment staging, specific play structures, significant landscaping changes, and the anticipated
impact of closures and construction on P.S. 84.

The following facts and concerns were considered in arriving at our conclusion:
The Swedish Cottage Marionette Theatre building (the “Marionette Theatre”) is situated within
Central Park, near Central Park West and the 79th street transverse. Community Board 7 considers the
Marionette Theatre a treasure and is in full support of the comprehensive restoration that it is
undergoing.
New York City Department of Parks & Recreation (“DPR”) has now approached CB7 with two
major proposed changes:
a. The proposal for the restoration of the staircases at the three entrance-bearing facades of the
Marionette Theatre (the north, south, and east facades): The staircases at all three facades have
experienced significant weathering and deterioration over the years, and this has extended to the
railings and balusters.
Detailed renderings of the several modifications that the Marionette Theatre has undergone
since 1876 are not available. As a result, DPR is proposing to replace the wooden railings with metal
ones, and does not believe that this exchange is in conflict with the original (unknown) design of the
Marionette Theatre. Wherever possible, the wooden posts and balusters will be restored or replaced
in kind, and the new metal railings that will serve the purpose of an ADA-compliant top rail, will be
attached. The metal will be solid bronze with a natural finish that will patina over time, requiring less
routine maintenance by DPR. A wood curve at the stair platform will also be added for fall protection
purposes.
The design and restoration work across all three entrances will follow the same pattern.
The decision by DPR to use metal railings instead of wooden ones is due to the longevity and
strength of the material and its ease of maintenance. While this design does not exactly match the
rustic nature of the Marionette Theatre, DPR also shared photos of various iterations of the design
that show no consistent intent or philosophy since the building was first constructed.
b. New Flagpoles: In order to comply with all proper flag protocols at the Marionette Theatre, DPR is
proposing two new flagpoles at the north entrance. One of these will fly the United States flag, while
the other will fly the flag of Sweden. The matte-finished aluminum flagpoles will be installed in-
ground, by the ADA ramp, and be lit at night. They will be 25 ft tall (about 1 ft in-ground), and will rise
lower than the 25.5 ft height of the roof ridge of the Marionette Theater.
The existing flagpole on top of the Marionette Theater will continue to fly the U.S. flag.
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7 approves the replacement of the wooden
railings with metal as proposed, as we find them to be minimally appropriate to the historic Marionette
Theatre and to Central Park, a NYC Scenic Landmark. However, CB7’s strong suggestion is for DPR to
explore alternative materials for the railings other than solid bronze, including long lasting wood such as
cedar or composites. We understand the desire to use a material that will last over time, weather well,
require less ongoing maintenance that is also less expensive, while also remaining within
budget. However, CB7 believes that the rustic, “log cabin” nature of the Marionette Theatre would be
enhanced by railings that match the rest of it in appearance and spirit, regardless of the material used.
FURTHER, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7 approves the in-kind restoration or
replacement of the wooden balusters as proposed, as we find them to be reasonably appropriate to the
historic Marionette Theatre and to Central Park.
FURTHER, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7 approves the installation of the two
new flagpoles as proposed, as we find them to be reasonably appropriate to the historic
Marionette Theater and to Central Park.

WHEREAS, Annual ridership has more than doubled since 2019 with 35 million Citi Bike rides in
2023 totaling 55 million miles, Citi Bike has become an invaluable resource for New York City residents;
and
WHEREAS, per-minute fees for acoustic bikes have increased 40% and e-bikes 60% from 2023 to
2024, the recent price hikes for Citi Bike memberships poses a significant barrier to accessibility for many
New York City students, hindering their ability to utilize this efficient mode of transportation; and
WHEREAS, the Reduced Fare Bike Share program introduced by Citi Bike in 2018 for NYCHA
residents and SNAP recipients has demonstrated success in expanding access to Citi Bike with around
16,000 residents participating in the Reduced Fare Bike Share Program; and
WHEREAS, the Reduced Fare Bike Share Program has been more consistently utilized with
members taking 77% more trips than regular Citi Bike members; and
WHEREAS, extending the $5 per month membership to include public high school and CUNY
students aged 16 and above would provide them with affordable access to Citi Bike, addressing the
challenges of long and inconvenient school commutes; and
WHEREAS, over 70 percent of students served by NYC Public Schools are economically
disadvantaged1 and half of all the students served by CUNY institutions come from households with
incomes less than $30,0002 underscores the urgent need for initiatives like Affordable Student Access to
Citi Bike to alleviate transportation burdens for students; and
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Community Board 7/ Manhattan for New York City hereby
endorse and support the initiative for Affordable Student Access to Citi Bike, advocating for the expansion
of the Reduced Fare Bike Share program to include public high school and CUNY students aged 16 and
above; and
THEREFORE, BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Community Board 7/ Manhattan urge Citi Bike to
work collaboratively with relevant city agencies and educational institutions to implement and administer
the Affordable Student Access to Citi Bike program effectively, ensuring its accessibility and affordability
for eligible students, and
THEREFORE, BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that that Community Board 7/ Manhattan urge Mayor
Adams, NYC Departments of Education and Transportation, and CUNY institutions to allocate necessary
resources and support for the implementation of this program, recognizing its potential to improve
student transportation options, reduce chronic absenteeism, promote physical activity, and enhance
academic performance among New York City students.

of encouragement and congratulations.

required by CB7’s Guidelines for secondary street co-naming’s.
• At the hearing, to the surprise of the Committee, oral presentations by other residents of the
same building presented markedly different accounts of Mr. Abolafia’s interactions with residents
and neighbors that detracted from the accounts on which the application was based. In
particular, two other residents described in unfortunate detail a consistent pattern of interactions
between Mr. Abolifia and certain residents of the building that included harsh language,
dismissive and belittling comments, and rude interjections on subjects that should not find their
way into casual conversation. The counter-presentations included such inappropriate comments
and subjects directed at children.
• The counter-presentation also included signatures of residents who joined in opposing the
Application.
• Community Boards are not adjudicative bodies. We cannot subpoena witnesses, conduct
investigations into the character of the subjects of applications such as this, or have a confident
basis on which to decide which of the competing portrayals of Mr. Abolifia is correct, or the closest
to the truth.
• In addition, while CB7 has in previous resolutions taken the position that secondary street co-
namings should be revisited after 10 years, it is our experience that once a street co-naming is
attached to a street pole, it remains there indefinitely. Therefore, street co-naming’s should
require a broad consensus that the individual subject of the application is worthy of such a
permanent honor.
• CB7 is unable to reach such a confident consensus with respect to Oscar Abolifia.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan is unable to offer a
recommendation either for or against the application for a secondary street co-naming of West 98th
Street in honor of Oscar Abolifia.

at one such event with the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Dr. King later nominated Thich Nhat
Hanh for a Nobel Peace Prize, the only individual Dr. King so nominated.
• Thich Nhat Hanh led the Buddhist delegation to the Paris Peace Talks, seeking an end to the Viet
Nam War.
• The author of over 100 books, including “Fragrant Palm Leaves” that chronicled his residence on
West 109th Street and at Columbia University, Thich Nhat Hanh shared his teachings and example
of mindfulness and focus on peace with the world.
• Thich Nhat Hanh’s artistry in calligraphy and the written word has inspired generations of
followers seeking a more just world built upon mindfulness and empathy.
• Adding a secondary street co-naming to the Southwest corner of West 109th Street and Broadway
would serve to honor an inspired advocate for peace in a community that can justly claim a
consistent activism in the advancement of the cause of peace and justice both at home and
throughout the world.

Re: Proposed resolution in support of NY State Senate Bill 2023-S8907A, which directs the department
of health to complete a report of the impact of hospital closures on healthcare access in the state.
Full Board

Vote: 32 In Favor 0 Against 0 Abstentions 0 Present
The following are considerations for supporting New York State Senate Bill 2023-S8907A:
• Hospitals serve as a critical foundation for healthcare delivery, providing essential services such
as emergency care, surgeries, maternal care, and specialized treatments that ensure the well-
being of all residents across New York State.
• Recent years have seen a troubling trend of hospital closures in certain regions of New York State,
particularly in underserved and rural areas, creating significant gaps in healthcare access and
exacerbating disparities in health outcomes for vulnerable populations.
• Hospital closures can negatively affect access to timely and quality medical care, increasing travel
time for patients, overburdening remaining healthcare facilities, and worsening health inequities,
especially for those with limited mobility, lower incomes, or chronic health conditions.
• There is a need for comprehensive and data-driven insights into the causes and consequences of
hospital closures, as well as their impact on healthcare access, quality, and outcomes in different
regions of New York State.
• Senate Bill 2023-S8907A aims to address this urgent issue by directing the New York State
Department of Health (DOH) to complete a thorough report on the impact of hospital closures on
healthcare access in the state, focusing on the specific challenges faced by communities that have
experienced or are at risk of such closures.
• The report mandated by Senate Bill 2023-S8907A will provide essential data and analysis to inform
future healthcare policy decisions, including potential actions to prevent hospital closures,
mitigate their effects, and improve access to healthcare services for all New Yorkers.
• The report will assess factors such as the availability of alternative healthcare resources (e.g.,
urgent care centers, primary care facilities), the impact on emergency medical services, the
availability of specialized care, and the broader socio-economic consequences of hospital closures
in communities.
• The findings from the report will enable policymakers to develop targeted strategies for improving
healthcare infrastructure, supporting community health initiatives, and fostering equitable access
to high-quality care for all New Yorkers, regardless of geographic location or economic status.
• Improving healthcare access and equity in New York State is essential to the overall health and
well-being of its residents, as well as the economic and social vitality of its communities.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Community Board 7 strongly support New York State Senate
Bill 2023-S8907A and urge its passage in order to provide the Department of Health with the resources
and mandate to assess the impact of hospital closures on healthcare access, and to use this information
to improve healthcare delivery and policy throughout the state; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that we call for the immediate and sustained implementation of the
findings and recommendations from the report to safeguard healthcare access for all New Yorkers, with
a particular focus on underserved and rural communities that have been disproportionately affected by
hospital closures; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that a copy of this resolution be transmitted to the Governor of New
York State, the New York State Senate, the Department of Health, and other relevant stakeholders, urging
them to prioritize the passage of Senate Bill 2023-S8907A and to continue their efforts to enhance the
quality, accessibility, and affordability of healthcare for all New Yorkers.

Committee of Origin: Parks & Environment
Re: Verdi Square lighting, irrigation, and accessibility improvements.
Full Board Vote: 30 In Favor 0 Against 0 Abstentions 0 Present
Committee: 9-0-0-0. Non-Committee Board Member: 3-0-1-0.
The following facts and concerns were considered in arriving at our conclusion:
Verdi Square is a transportation hub and small park bordered by West 73rd Street on the north,
Amsterdam Avenue on the east, West 72nd Street on the south, and Broadway on the west. The western
half of the park, which encompasses the subway, is managed by the Metropolitan Transportation
Authority (MTA) and the Department of Transportation (DOT), while the eastern half of the park is
managed by DPR ("Verdi Square Park").
On December 16, 2024, the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation (DPR) presented
a plan (the “Plan”) to the MCB7 Parks & Environment Committee for the installation of water service,
improved lighting, and an improved, accessible pathway into the park and seating area within Verdi
Square. According to the Plan, the goals of this project are to:
• Provide water service and irrigation for gardens on both sides of Verdi Square. Currently, Verdi
Square lacks an irrigation system and consistent water source, requiring water to be manually
brought in via hoses. The Plan proposes installing a Reduced Pressure Zone (RPZ) backflow device,
a water meter, and a coupler at the corner of Amsterdam and West 73rd St and to bring in water
service supplied from the existing West 73rd St and Broadway water line. The Plan also proposes
installing a coupler in the northwestern section of Verdi Square to irrigate the garden there.
• Install ADA-accessible entrances and an asphalt path in the seating area behind Verdi Square Park.
The current pathways are covered with portable non-slip roll-out mats and are accessible only via
a temporary plywood ramp. The Plan proposes installing a new asphalt pathway over contracted
subgrade, bordered by gravel on both sides. The Plan also proposes that the pathway be flush
with the sidewalk, eliminating the raised curb, to make it ADA-accessible. New garden rails will be
installed on some edges near the seating area.
• Improve current lighting and install additional light poles to improve overall illumination in the
park. Verdi Square has experienced inadequate lighting and illumination, particularly near the
northern entrance of the subway and along the seating area in the park, creating public safety
concerns due to frequent drug use, loitering, and public urination in this immediate area. The Plan
proposes upgrading the existing light poles to LED luminaires. Additionally, the Plan proposes the
installation of six new LED light poles with the same luminaire design: four to be placed along the
seating area in Verdi Square Park, and two above the MTA tunnel.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Community Board 7/ Manhattan enthusiastically supports and
approves the Plan as presented for the installation of water service, lighting, and an improved ADA-
accessible pathway at Verdi Square. The Board believes that these positive changes will significantly
enhance the experience of visitors and commuters alike, while improving safety. The Board requests that
lighting enhancements above the northern subway entrance be prioritized, with a possible interim and
immediate solution being brighter temporary lighting. Furthermore, the Board requests that DPR explore
alternative materials to asphalt and gravel for the pathway, as there are concerns about potential
deterioration from the movement of heavy park chairs and tables.

Committee of Origin: Parks & Environment
Re: Verdi Square lighting, irrigation, and accessibility improvements.
Full Board Vote: 30 In Favor 0 Against 0 Abstentions 0 Present
Committee: 9-0-0-0. Non-Committee Board Member: 3-0-1-0.
The following facts and concerns were considered in arriving at our conclusion:
Verdi Square is a transportation hub and small park bordered by West 73rd Street on the north,
Amsterdam Avenue on the east, West 72nd Street on the south, and Broadway on the west. The western
half of the park, which encompasses the subway, is managed by the Metropolitan Transportation
Authority (MTA) and the Department of Transportation (DOT), while the eastern half of the park is
managed by DPR ("Verdi Square Park").
On December 16, 2024, the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation (DPR) presented
a plan (the “Plan”) to the MCB7 Parks & Environment Committee for the installation of water service,
improved lighting, and an improved, accessible pathway into the park and seating area within Verdi
Square. According to the Plan, the goals of this project are to:
• Provide water service and irrigation for gardens on both sides of Verdi Square. Currently, Verdi
Square lacks an irrigation system and consistent water source, requiring water to be manually
brought in via hoses. The Plan proposes installing a Reduced Pressure Zone (RPZ) backflow device,
a water meter, and a coupler at the corner of Amsterdam and West 73rd St and to bring in water
service supplied from the existing West 73rd St and Broadway water line. The Plan also proposes
installing a coupler in the northwestern section of Verdi Square to irrigate the garden there.
• Install ADA-accessible entrances and an asphalt path in the seating area behind Verdi Square Park.
The current pathways are covered with portable non-slip roll-out mats and are accessible only via
a temporary plywood ramp. The Plan proposes installing a new asphalt pathway over contracted
subgrade, bordered by gravel on both sides. The Plan also proposes that the pathway be flush
with the sidewalk, eliminating the raised curb, to make it ADA-accessible. New garden rails will be
installed on some edges near the seating area.
• Improve current lighting and install additional light poles to improve overall illumination in the
park. Verdi Square has experienced inadequate lighting and illumination, particularly near the
northern entrance of the subway and along the seating area in the park, creating public safety
concerns due to frequent drug use, loitering, and public urination in this immediate area. The Plan
proposes upgrading the existing light poles to LED luminaires. Additionally, the Plan proposes the
installation of six new LED light poles with the same luminaire design: four to be placed along the
seating area in Verdi Square Park, and two above the MTA tunnel.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Community Board 7/ Manhattan enthusiastically supports and
approves the Plan as presented for the installation of water service, lighting, and an improved ADA-
accessible pathway at Verdi Square. The Board believes that these positive changes will significantly
enhance the experience of visitors and commuters alike, while improving safety. The Board requests that
lighting enhancements above the northern subway entrance be prioritized, with a possible interim and
immediate solution being brighter temporary lighting. Furthermore, the Board requests that DPR explore
alternative materials to asphalt and gravel for the pathway, as there are concerns about potential
deterioration from the movement of heavy park chairs and tables.

Committee of Origin: Parks & Environment
Re: Verdi Square lighting, irrigation, and accessibility improvements.
Full Board Vote: 30 In Favor 0 Against 0 Abstentions 0 Present
Committee: 9-0-0-0. Non-Committee Board Member: 3-0-1-0.
The following facts and concerns were considered in arriving at our conclusion:
Verdi Square is a transportation hub and small park bordered by West 73rd Street on the north,
Amsterdam Avenue on the east, West 72nd Street on the south, and Broadway on the west. The western
half of the park, which encompasses the subway, is managed by the Metropolitan Transportation
Authority (MTA) and the Department of Transportation (DOT), while the eastern half of the park is
managed by DPR ("Verdi Square Park").
On December 16, 2024, the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation (DPR) presented
a plan (the “Plan”) to the MCB7 Parks & Environment Committee for the installation of water service,
improved lighting, and an improved, accessible pathway into the park and seating area within Verdi
Square. According to the Plan, the goals of this project are to:
• Provide water service and irrigation for gardens on both sides of Verdi Square. Currently, Verdi
Square lacks an irrigation system and consistent water source, requiring water to be manually
brought in via hoses. The Plan proposes installing a Reduced Pressure Zone (RPZ) backflow device,
a water meter, and a coupler at the corner of Amsterdam and West 73rd St and to bring in water
service supplied from the existing West 73rd St and Broadway water line. The Plan also proposes
installing a coupler in the northwestern section of Verdi Square to irrigate the garden there.
• Install ADA-accessible entrances and an asphalt path in the seating area behind Verdi Square Park.
The current pathways are covered with portable non-slip roll-out mats and are accessible only via
a temporary plywood ramp. The Plan proposes installing a new asphalt pathway over contracted
subgrade, bordered by gravel on both sides. The Plan also proposes that the pathway be flush
with the sidewalk, eliminating the raised curb, to make it ADA-accessible. New garden rails will be
installed on some edges near the seating area.
• Improve current lighting and install additional light poles to improve overall illumination in the
park. Verdi Square has experienced inadequate lighting and illumination, particularly near the
northern entrance of the subway and along the seating area in the park, creating public safety
concerns due to frequent drug use, loitering, and public urination in this immediate area. The Plan
proposes upgrading the existing light poles to LED luminaires. Additionally, the Plan proposes the
installation of six new LED light poles with the same luminaire design: four to be placed along the
seating area in Verdi Square Park, and two above the MTA tunnel.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Community Board 7/ Manhattan enthusiastically supports and
approves the Plan as presented for the installation of water service, lighting, and an improved ADA-
accessible pathway at Verdi Square. The Board believes that these positive changes will significantly
enhance the experience of visitors and commuters alike, while improving safety. The Board requests that
lighting enhancements above the northern subway entrance be prioritized, with a possible interim and
immediate solution being brighter temporary lighting. Furthermore, the Board requests that DPR explore
alternative materials to asphalt and gravel for the pathway, as there are concerns about potential
deterioration from the movement of heavy park chairs and tables.

Re: Verdi Square lighting, irrigation, and accessibility improvements.
Full Board Vote: 30 In Favor 0 Against 0 Abstentions 0 Present
Committee: 9-0-0-0. Non-Committee Board Member: 3-0-1-0.
The following facts and concerns were considered in arriving at our conclusion:
Verdi Square is a transportation hub and small park bordered by West 73rd Street on the north,
Amsterdam Avenue on the east, West 72nd Street on the south, and Broadway on the west. The western
half of the park, which encompasses the subway, is managed by the Metropolitan Transportation
Authority (MTA) and the Department of Transportation (DOT), while the eastern half of the park is
managed by DPR ("Verdi Square Park").
On December 16, 2024, the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation (DPR) presented
a plan (the “Plan”) to the MCB7 Parks & Environment Committee for the installation of water service,
improved lighting, and an improved, accessible pathway into the park and seating area within Verdi
Square. According to the Plan, the goals of this project are to:
• Provide water service and irrigation for gardens on both sides of Verdi Square. Currently, Verdi
Square lacks an irrigation system and consistent water source, requiring water to be manually
brought in via hoses. The Plan proposes installing a Reduced Pressure Zone (RPZ) backflow device,
a water meter, and a coupler at the corner of Amsterdam and West 73rd St and to bring in water
service supplied from the existing West 73rd St and Broadway water line. The Plan also proposes
installing a coupler in the northwestern section of Verdi Square to irrigate the garden there.
• Install ADA-accessible entrances and an asphalt path in the seating area behind Verdi Square Park.
The current pathways are covered with portable non-slip roll-out mats and are accessible only via
a temporary plywood ramp. The Plan proposes installing a new asphalt pathway over contracted
subgrade, bordered by gravel on both sides. The Plan also proposes that the pathway be flush
with the sidewalk, eliminating the raised curb, to make it ADA-accessible. New garden rails will be
installed on some edges near the seating area.
• Improve current lighting and install additional light poles to improve overall illumination in the
park. Verdi Square has experienced inadequate lighting and illumination, particularly near the
northern entrance of the subway and along the seating area in the park, creating public safety
concerns due to frequent drug use, loitering, and public urination in this immediate area. The Plan
proposes upgrading the existing light poles to LED luminaires. Additionally, the Plan proposes the
installation of six new LED light poles with the same luminaire design: four to be placed along the
seating area in Verdi Square Park, and two above the MTA tunnel.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Community Board 7/ Manhattan enthusiastically supports and
approves the Plan as presented for the installation of water service, lighting, and an improved ADA-
accessible pathway at Verdi Square. The Board believes that these positive changes will significantly
enhance the experience of visitors and commuters alike, while improving safety. The Board requests that
lighting enhancements above the northern subway entrance be prioritized, with a possible interim and
immediate solution being brighter temporary lighting. Furthermore, the Board requests that DPR explore
alternative materials to asphalt and gravel for the pathway, as there are concerns about potential
deterioration from the movement of heavy park chairs and tables.

district, and encourages property owners, businesses and stakeholders to participate in this effort.

Broadway Mall Association, property owners and other stakeholders to explore the possibility of creating
a Broadway BID.

measures regarding requests for secondary street co-naming:

signatures of the total residents and/or businesses within two blocks of the secondary street to
be co-named. Petitions must include the names, addresses, dates of signature, and signatures of
the signatory. For individual honorees, applications for secondary street co-naming must include
proof that members of the family of the individual to be honored do not object to the secondary
street co-naming.

secondary street co-naming, including:
i. the proposed honoree;
ii. the reason(s) for the honor;
iii. the proposed location; and
iv. how to make a public comment on the proposed honoree and/or location.
C. Applicants must certify and describe their efforts to secure a plaque or other commemoration on
a building, sidewalk, lamp post or other appropriate space on the designated street prior to
submitting a request for a secondary street co-naming.
D. Individual honorees must:
i. Have been deceased for at least 10 years; and
ii. Have had an extraordinary and highly acclaimed accomplishment or involvement for
the public good linked to MCB7 and the street proposed for the co-naming; or
iii. Have been a key person in an event of historical note, including individuals whose
death occurred under extraordinary circumstances of crime, accident, disease or a
societal problem if their death led to a greater awareness within society of that issue;
or
iv. Have brought about significant changes through their involvement in MCB7.
E. Non-Profit honorees must:
i. Have demonstrated an extraordinary and continuous commitment of at least 20 years
that has benefited the community and/or community members in MCB7; and
ii. Be located on the street proposed for co-naming; or

The following facts were taken into account when considering this resolution:
WHEREAS, numerous residents and neighborhood groups, including the West 71st Street Block
Association, have come before MCB7 to inquire about congestion and streetscape design along the 70th-
72nd superblock along Amsterdam Avenue; and
WHEREAS, the current bike corral at the southwest corner of 71st and Amsterdam, located within
the superblock, is in an area that experiences significant pedestrian activity, increasing congestion and
traffic; and
WHEREAS, the current bike corral experiences significant overcrowding of parked, locked bikes
often for extended periods of time; and
WHEREAS, this part of the neighborhood is not at present served by a Business Improvement
District.

Transportation to:
• Remove the bike racks/corral on the southwest corner of 71st St and Amsterdam Avenue
sidewalk, and
• Move the bike racks/corral to the curb on Amsterdam Avenue and 71st St, or to an alternative,
more efficient location nearby, and
• Ensure the new bike racks/corral can safely accommodate an equal or greater number of
bicycles

The following informs our support of the H.E.L.P. Act, sponsored by State Senator Brad
Hoylman-Sigal and State Assemblymember Micah Lasher:
The mental health crisis in New York City has reached alarming levels, with individuals
struggling with mental illness often left without the necessary care and support.
The closure of thousands of mental health beds across the state over the last several
decades has exacerbated this crisis, leading to individuals languishing on the streets and in the
subways.
The H.E.L.P. Act (Harness Expertise of Licensed Professionals) aims to address this crisis
by expanding the pool of mental health professionals authorized to perform clinical evaluations
for involuntary hospitalization and assisted outpatient treatment.
The H.E.L.P. Act would allow not only physicians but also psychiatric nurse practitioners,
psychologists, and clinical social workers to perform these evaluations, thereby alleviating the
systemic staffing shortage and ensuring patients receive timely care.
The H.E.L.P. Act requires hospital administrators to notify community mental health
providers when a patient is admitted or discharged, ensuring better continuity of care and
coordination between different layers of the healthcare system.
In addition, while the H.E.L.P. Act will address a crucial problem, the mental health
services needed will not be met unless there is also an accompanying plan for more inpatient
psychiatric beds to meet the growing need.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Community Board 7 / Manhattan expresses our strong
support for the H.E.L.P. Act and urges the New York State Legislature and Governor Hochul to
pass this crucial legislation to improve mental health services and protect the well-being of our
community.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Community Board 7 urges the New York State Legislature
and Governor Hochul at the same time to address the need for restoration and expansion of the
inpatient psychiatric bed capacity, as the demand continues to outpace the supply.

Date: February 4, 2025
Committee of Origin: Transportation
Re: Plastic Bollard placement and safety along UWS avenues.
Full Board Vote: 35 In Favor 0 Against 1 Abstentions 0 Present
The following facts were taken into consideration:
The white, flexible bollards that the city currently uses to separate traffic often break and
lay flat on the road semi-attached to their base. These pose a serious tripping hazard for
pedestrians and can easily cause a cyclist to lose their balance and fall, risking harm to them and
other street users. The bollards also attract dirt, causing them to be unsightly and less visible on
the ground at night. Furthermore, they often fail to achieve their purpose of separating street
users due to their vulnerability. Most other cities use durable metal posts to separate street
traffic, presumably for these very reasons.
THEREFORE, Community Board 7/ Manhattan resolves that the city should cease using
flexible bollards and instead use more durable posts to separate street traffic.

The following facts and concerns were taken into account in arriving at our conclusions:
• NYC Health & Hospitals/Bellevue plays a vital role as a tertiary care hospital within the
New York City Health and Hospitals Corporation (HHC), serving as a referral center for
complex and specialized care across the entire HHC system and providing critical services
to New York City communities;
• NYC Health & Hospitals/Bellevue is a cornerstone of the public health care system in New
York City, providing care to hundreds of thousands of patients annually and serving as a
lifeline for many of the city’s most vulnerable residents, including Medicaid beneficiaries,
uninsured individuals, and those unable to access care elsewhere;
• The anticipated closure of Mount Sinai Beth Israel Hospital is expected to increase patient
demand at Bellevue across all areas of care, including emergency services, inpatient and
outpatient treatment, and specialized behavioral health services, straining Bellevue’s
resources and further challenging its ability to meet the needs of the community;
• Mount Sinai Beth Israel has historically maintained a strong and comprehensive
behavioral health program, and its closure will disproportionately impact patients seeking
behavioral health services, many of whom are expected to rely on Bellevue as a safety
net provider in the absence of other accessible options;
• As a public hospital, NYC Health & Hospitals/Bellevue is mandated to treat all patients
regardless of their ability to pay, demonstrating an unwavering commitment to health
equity and access, while carrying the financial burden of uncompensated care and low
reimbursement rates that disproportionately affect safety net hospitals;
• Approximately 60% of patients at Bellevue are insured through Medicaid, a program that
currently reimburses hospitals at only 70% of the actual cost of care, creating a persistent
funding gap that places immense financial strain on Bellevue and other safety net
providers across New York City;
• The inadequate reimbursement rates for Medicaid fail to account for the true costs of
care delivery, including rising operational costs, the increasing complexity of medical
cases, and the growing demand for services, particularly in areas with limited access to
private health care providers;
• Safety net hospitals like Bellevue are forced to rely on government bailouts, emergency
funding measures, and other reactive strategies to address operational budget deficits
caused by insufficient Medicaid reimbursements, which is far less efficient than providing
sustainable funding through upfront reimbursement that reflects the true cost of care;
• Insufficient Medicaid funding creates systemic inequities in health care delivery by
underfunding hospitals that serve marginalized and underserved communities,
effectively perpetuating disparities in health outcomes and access to care;

1. Re: Support for NYS Discovery Law Amendments – Assembly Bill A825 / Senate Bill S613.
The following information was taken into consideration:
• The legislature enacted reforms in 2020 in order to enhance transparency and fairness in criminal proceedings by
ensuring timely access to evidence for defendants. However, some of these reforms have burdened district
attorneys’ offices and law enforcement agencies with tight deadlines for record collection and disclosure. The lack
of direct access by district attorneys to law enforcement evidence systems forced prosecutors to rely on a manual
and delayed process;
• This act aims to improve the efficiency of the criminal discovery process by granting district attorneys’ offices
direct access to law enforcement records and databases. It requires police departments and agencies to provide
login credentials to district attorneys’ offices, allowing them to access relevant information related to criminal
cases. The act seeks to alleviate delays, reduce administrative burdens, and ensure fair resolution of cases;
• To address these challenges, this act seeks to improve discovery efficiency by granting direct access to law
enforcement records and databases related to criminal cases. This access will alleviate delays, reduce
administrative burdens, and ensure cases are resolved based on merits rather than procedural failures. By
allowing staff to retrieve records, the act aims to return police officers to their core responsibilities of public safety;
• The legislature believes these reforms will promote timely and fair criminal case resolution, advancing justice for
defendants and the public; and
• The Legal Aid Society of New York Supports these Bills.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7 / Manhattan supports the passage of these two Bills, at the
NY State Assembly and NY State Senate, respectively.

2. Re: Resolution Urging the NYC Comptroller and Chief Investment Officer of the NYC Public Pension Funds to
Promote Workplace Equity and Inclusion.
WHEREAS, The New York City Public Pension Funds (NYCPPF) manage approximately $280 billion in
assets, making it the third-largest city pension system in the United States; and
WHEREAS, The New York City Comptroller’s Office, as a long-time steward of public investments, has
both a fiduciary duty and a moral obligation to ensure that financial commitments align with principles of
inclusivity, fairness, and responsible corporate governance; and

entities to eliminate or scale back programs that have the potential to create a more equitable, merit-based and
inclusive workplace pose a risk to the long-term financial growth and innovation of these businesses, thereby
potentially impacting the returns of the NYCPPF and other institutional investors; and

sustainability; and

3. Re: Renovation Project for Frederick Douglass Playground by NYC Parks
The following facts and concerns were considered in arriving at our conclusion:
Frederick Douglass Playground (the Playground) is located on Amsterdam Avenue between West 100th and West
101st Streets. The Playground includes modular play equipment, swings, safety surfacing, a handball court, a camel play
structure, and a basketball court. The synthetic turf field, the mini-pool and the bathrooms within the Playground are not
included in the scope of this reconstruction.
The Playground is currently outdated, worn, damaged by years of inclement weather, and lacks accessibility and
sustainability. On March 17, 2025, the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation (DPR) presented a plan (the
Plan) to the MCB7 Parks & Environment Committee (the Committee) for the reconstruction of the Playground.
According to the Plan, the goals of this reconstruction are the following:
• Make the Playground an improved facility for the community. The Plan is based partly on DPR’s community
outreach where input was collected from local residents. Community priorities included water play features,
better screening and tree coverage, better seating, making play accessible, inclusive, colorful and sensory, and
improved safety and circulation.
• Improve site safety and circulation. The Playground currently lacks adequate lighting and has awkward circulation
paths, creating safety hazards. Additionally, only two of the Playground's three entrances are open. The
reconstruction will reopen all three entrances, add additional lighting, lower the fences, and introduce a new Tot
Lot – a designated, protected play area for caregivers and toddlers.
• Enhance environmental amenities of the site. The reconstruction will incorporate sustainable practices, such as
increasing permeable surfaces, using recycled materials, improving tree health and growing conditions, planting
resilient and site-appropriate plant species, and activating spray showers only on demand.
• Provide play features for users of all abilities and sensory needs. The Plan includes new accessible and inclusive
play equipment, benches, game tables, and spray features, among others. It will also add colorful pavement
graphics and reimagine the Playground’s layout to improve circulation, accessibility, and overall functionality.
The Committee found the Plan to be thoughtful, imaginative and colorful and commended the Plan’s focus on
safety, sustainability and accessibility. Further, the Committee appreciated the community outreach conducted by DPR in
anticipation of this reconstruction and the subsequent incorporation of community input.

5. Re: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (MET), Central Park. Application to the:
a. Public Design Commission by the Department of Parks & Recreation and the Central Park Conservancy for
landscaping.
The following facts and concerns were considered in arriving at our conclusion:
The Metropolitan Museum of Art (the Met or the Museum) is proposing the replacement of one wing
in its existing building complex on Fifth Avenue, within Central Park (the Park). The new wing is designed by
Mexican architect Frida Escobedo and will be called the Oscar L. Tang and H.M. Agnes Hsu-Tang Wing (the
Tang Wing) for Modern and Contemporary Art.
The Tang Wing would be a five-story structure, approximately 163,100 gross square foot (gsf) in size
and 124,900 gsf above grade. It will be integrated into the southwest corner of the Museum’s current
building complex, replacing the existing Lila Acheson Wallace (LAW) Wing at this location.
The landscaping design plan is focused on the south-west corner of the Museum, outside the
proposed Tang Wing. The Central Park Conservancy (CPC) is responsible for the design, and it will work with
the NYC Department of Parks & Recreation (DPR) for its implementation. This is the first major redesign
effort since the 1980s Master Plan by DPR.
According to the proposed plan, the goals of this project are to:
• Improve accessibility to enhance the Park user experience.
• Refine the landscape quality and character.
• Improve the interface between the Park and the Museum.
To enhance the interface between the Museum and the Park and improve accessibility, the pathway
at this site will be relocated slightly and re-graded. This adjustment will make the pathway fully ADA-
accessible from Fifth Avenue till the Great Lawn. The proposed plan will also improve the loading access,
which is currently located at the edge of the building, at Petrie Court.
As a result of the regrading, the project will unfortunately necessitate the removal of 13 trees and the
transplantation of 2 trees. In response, CPC expects to plant 40-50 new trees. The landscaping plan also
includes planting a diverse understory around the proposed building to create visual appeal and improve

The following facts were taken into consideration:
A. The Second Look Act:
The following facts and concerns were taken into account in arriving at our conclusions:
● Decades-long prison terms have become increasingly common in New York State. Every
year, nearly 1,000 people are sentenced to 10 or more years in prison, and over 5,000
people—more than 10 percent of people in prison—have been there for 15 years or
longer;
● New York State has the third-largest population of people serving terms of life
imprisonment in the country. Nearly 9,000 New Yorkers are currently serving life
sentences;
● Prisons have become de facto hospitals and long-term care facilities for thousands of sick
and aging people;
● This increase in sentence length stems primarily from the “tough-on-crime” laws passed
in the 1970s and 1990s, which disproportionately targeted Black and brown communities;
● Those who are serving lengthy sentences have no opportunity to demonstrate to a judge
that they have changed after years or decades in prison or that, given new laws and
revised norms, the sentence is no longer appropriate;
● Judges have spoken out about their inability to address sentences that are extreme or
unjust;
● The Second Look Act (S.158 - Salazar / A.1283 - Walker) allows incarcerated people to
petition for resentencing and permits judges to revisit and reduce excessive sentences;
● Cases will be heard by a different judge than the initial sentencing judge;
● Incarcerated people may apply for a resentencing hearing after they have served 10 years
or half of their sentence (if the sentence is over a decade). If a person is otherwise
ineligible, the prosecutor can consent to their resentencing application.
● The Second Look Act creates a presumption that resentencing will be granted if the
person is over 55 years old at the time of the resentencing hearing, or was under 25 years
old at the time the crime occurred;
● The right to counsel is guaranteed at every stage of second look proceedings; and
● Nationally, second look bills are gaining momentum with legislation passed in four
states— Illinois, Louisiana, Maryland, Oregon—and the District of Columbia, and
proposed in an additional 22 states. Federally, U.S. Senator Cory Booker has proposed
second look legislation in Congress.

B. The Earned Time Act:
The following facts and concerns were taken into account in arriving at our conclusions:
● Despite research finding that longer prison sentences do not reduce crime or improve
safety, until now New York State has focused on warehousing people in prison rather than
rehabilitation;
● Good time and merit time programs are found to support personal transformation by
encouraging participation in education, employment, and other rehabilitative programs
that promote the criminal legal system’s goal of rehabilitation, reduce recidivism and
promote positive post-release outcomes;
● During the 1990s, New York State slashed programs for incarcerated people and
substantially limited the time people could earn off their sentences. This included
eliminating financial aid for incarcerated college students and decimating college-in
prison programs;
● New York also restricted access to merit time based on the type of conviction, while at
the same time eliminating key opportunities for rehabilitative programming and earned
time for thousands of New Yorkers each year;
● Research shows that earned time opportunities help to prepare incarcerated people for
reintegration, reduce recidivism rates and correctional costs;
● New York trails other states---including some traditionally conservative states---on
allowing incarcerated people to earn time off their sentences;
● Current State law fails to provide incarcerated people with meaningful opportunities to
earn release and gives the New York State Department of Corrections and Community
Supervision unlimited discretion to deny earned good time and merit time credits---even
after years of good conduct;
● The Earned Time Act (S. 342 – Cooney/A.1085 – Kelles) will strengthen good time and
merit time allowance credits in relation to early release of incarcerated individuals;
● Earned time helps to prepare incarcerated people for reintegration and to restore them
to their families and communities. The Act will strengthen and expand good time and
merit time laws to encourage personal transformation in prison and reunite families;
● The Act allows all incarcerated people to earn good time and merit time, so that all
incarcerated people---regardless of conviction---have the opportunity and
encouragement to engage in personal transformation; and
● It expands opportunities for earning merit time and incentivizes individual prisons to offer
the strongest rehabilitative programs.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan expresses our strong
support for the Earned Time Act and urges the New York State Legislature to pass and Governor
Hochul to sign this common-sense reform.

On May 20, 2024, the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation (“DPR”) presented a
comprehensive plan for the reconstruction of the Soldiers and Sailors Monument (the "Monument"),
located in Riverside Park (the "Park"). The plan detailed the restoration of the Monument and proposed
modifications to ensure ADA-compliant accessibility. This plan was approved at the Manhattan
Community Board 7 (the “Board”) Full Board Meeting on June 4, 2024, and subsequently by the Landmark
Preservation Commission on June 11, 2024.
As survey work on the Monument continues, DPR returned on April 21, 2025 with a proposal to
improve the lighting of the Monument’s façade and surrounding area, as well as to upgrade its utility
infrastructure.
In this proposal, DPR specifically presented the following goals:
● Improve Lighting. The existing lighting system is outdated and relies on inefficient fixtures that do
not provide adequate illumination to the Monument’s architectural details or surroundings,
especially at night. The Park is also a habitat to numerous resident and migratory bird species,
and the current system produces light that can be disorienting to birds, especially to those on
their migratory journey. The Plan addresses these issues by removing the DOT street poles with
floodlights and replacing them with programmable LED luminaires. The Plan also proposes new
lighting that can be dynamically programmed to seasonal changes, and installing maintenance-
friendly fixtures and controls. Further, based on recommendations from the New York Bird
Alliance, the new design will mitigate light trespass to reduce impacts to birds.

these updates, while also being sensitive to scenic views of the Monument. Specifically, new
metered electrical service will be installed to power the architectural lighting, along with new
water service lines equipped with Reduced Pressure Zone (RPZ) devices. This new system will be
screened from views by plantings carefully chosen to conceal the utilities and will not detract from
views of the Monument.
The Board appreciates the carefully considered lighting and utility updates centered on
minimizing impacts to resident and migratory bird species, while ensuring that the Monument’s intended
viewing experience and character are well preserved. We especially appreciate DPR’s engagement with
the New York Bird Alliance to develop bird-friendly lighting practices, and the selection of native, site-

Full Board

Vote: 36 In Favor 0 Against 0 Abstentions 0 Present
Committee: 8-0-0-1.
The following facts and concerns were taken into account in arriving at our conclusions:
The proliferation of nonessential helicopter flights—including sightseeing tours, private
commuter flights and luxury charters—has led to significant concerns among residents about persistent
noise pollution, public safety risks, and environmental impacts;
Helicopter noise has been consistently cited by New York City residents as a major quality-of-life
issue, particularly in Manhattan, Brooklyn, Staten Island, and along the Hudson and East rivers;
Since 2000, a nonessential helicopter has crashed on average every two years in the New York
City area, with several recent high-profile crashes underscoring the tragic consequences of such flights;
Nonessential helicopters put unnecessary strain on the already overburdened traffic control
system in highly congested New York City airspace;
These flights disproportionately benefit a small number of individuals while imposing costs in the
form of noise, safety risks, property value reductions, and environmental degradation on the broader
population;
Helicopter fuel emissions contribute to air pollution and climate change, in contradiction to the
City’s stated goals of reducing greenhouse gas emissions and creating a more sustainable urban
environment;
NYC 311 received more than 26,000 helicopter noise complaints in 2024, the majority of which
originated from the Upper West Side – an average of 40 complaints per day;
On January 7, 2020, CB7’s full board voted unanimously to support “our elected officials’ efforts
to reduce helicopter traffic in the city, including the enactment of the Improving Helicopter Safety Act of
2019 (HR 4880), which would have prohibited nonessential helicopter flights from flying within New York
City airspace; and
On January 5, 2021, CB7’s full board voted unanimously in support of a resolution calling on the
City to cease using taxpayer funds to promote helicopter tours that are the cause of escalating community
noise complaints and other concerns.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan supports and urges passage
of several bills that have been introduced at the city, state and federal levels that would ban or reduce
nonessential helicopter flights over the New York City metropolitan area. These bills are:
● H.R. 3196, the Improving Helicopter Safety Act of 2025, which prohibits nonessential
helicopter flights within a 20-mile radius of the Statue of Liberty National Monument.
● NY City Council Int. 0070-2024, which prohibits all nonessential helicopter operations at
heliports owned or operated by NYC.
● NYS Senate Bill S7381/NYS Assembly Bill A6311, which bans helicopter sightseeing tours from
any municipal facility.
● NYS Senate Bill S1140 / NYS Assembly Bill A5891, which establishes a tax on noise from
nonessential helicopter and seaplane flights in cities with a population of one million or more.
This bill would levy a tax of $50/seat or $200 /flight, whichever is greater.
● NYS Assembly Bill A2583, which establishes a tax on noise from nonessential helicopter and
seaplane flights in cities with a population of one million or more. This bill would levy a tax of
$100/seat or $400/flight, whichever is greater.
