Full Board

Vote: 28 In Favor 2 Against 5 Abstentions 0 Present
Committee: 5-1-3-0. Non-Committee Board Member: 0-0-1-0.
The following facts and concerns were taken into account in arriving at our conclusions:
On April 28, 2025, the NYPD began the practice of issuing criminal summonses to cyclists for
infractions like going through a red light, failing to stop at a stop sign, or riding on the sidewalk. Until that
time, cyclists, like drivers, were subject to a traffic ticket, which can be paid or contested online.
The drivers of cars and trucks continue to face only a ticket for violations like red-light running,
failing to stop at a stop sign, or speeding.
Being issued a criminal summons requires appearing in criminal court, which could conceivably
lead to a criminal record or jail. Those who fail to appear will likely have a warrant for their arrest issued.
For cyclists who are not citizens of the United States, which is the case for many delivery workers,
encounters with the criminal justice system are highly dangerous under the current federal government.
Such encounters could result in detention, deportation, or even indefinite imprisonment in a
foreign country – without any due process. In addition, an encounter with the criminal justice system
could jeopardize an application for asylum seeker status.
Despite New York being a “sanctuary city,” Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) can learn
of a cyclist receiving a summons because a criminal case, unlike a traffic ticket, is public information.
The practice begun in April 2025 is in response to 311 complaints and 911 calls about “out of
control e-bikes and scooters,” according to police commissioner Jessica Tisch.
Of the 9,610 New York City pedestrians injured in 2024, significantly less than one percent (37)
involved e-bike collisions, according to NYPD data. The other 99.6 percent of pedestrians were injured by
drivers of motor vehicles.
In 2023, 103 pedestrians were killed on New York City streets. Of these, 101 were killed in
collisions with cars, trucks or other motorized vehicles. Two were killed in collisions with cyclists.
An e-bike weighs between 40 and 80 pounds. A regular bike weighs between 20 and 40 pounds.
Cars weigh between 2,500 and 6,000 pounds. A loaded garbage truck weighs between 50,000
and 100,000 pounds.
The NYPD has a history of issuing criminal summonses for bike operation overwhelmingly to
cyclists of color. Last year, 95 percent of criminal summonses for sidewalk riding were issued to Black or
brown New Yorkers, and 92 percent of criminal summonses for reckless bike operation went to New
Yorkers of color.
According to news reports, in the last three weeks cyclists have received criminal summonses for
such things as wearing headphones, stopping just ahead of the painted stop line, and for proceeding at
the Leading Pedestrian Interval, which has been legal for cyclists to do in New York City since 2019.
The behavior on the streets from some cyclists is a problem. We agree with Commissioner Tisch
that this behavior is an issue that needs to be addressed.
MCB7 believes that holding cyclists to a far higher standard than motor vehicle drivers is unjust,
puts immigrant workers at grave risk, and sends the wrong message about the actual danger on our
streets.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan calls on the NYPD to
immediately end the practice of issuing criminal court summonses to cyclists for traffic violations and to
find another way to mitigate bad behavior. MCB7 also calls on elected officials including our City Council
to enact legislation to curb lawless behavior.

A. The Bethesda Terrace Restoration
Bethesda Terrace is located in Central Park just north of the 72nd street cross drive and
is most distinctly recognized by its iconic Fountain. Due to extensive wear and tear over decades,
the Terrace is in need of a comprehensive restoration. The goals of this project are to mechanize
fountain systems to improve performance and ease of maintenance, to address areas of
deterioration and code compliance, and to restore the historic features of the fountain.
● The sculpture and bronze features of the Fountain: The bronze applique below the putti
will be restored, the bronze lip at the middle basin will be cleaned and replaced as will
the floral bronze caps, while issues with staining on the underlying granite will also be
addressed. The floral bronze caps will be replaced for water flow along the middle lip as
well. A bronze flower applique feature that has unfortunately been lost over time will be
replaced in the original design.
● The Basin of the Fountain: The cracked concrete basin of the water fountain will be
replaced and waterproofed in-kind. The existing basin walls have thickened over time
due to added concrete layers, and will now be restored to their original level.
● Systems: For an upgrade of the systems supporting the fountain, three new structures
will be added next to existing ones that are north-east of Bethesda Terrace. These are
the underground filtration vault, the RPZ vault to prevent backflow, and an electrical
closet to control and power the new equipment. The majority of these structures will
exist below ground, and anything above ground will be hidden by new plantings in the
immediate area.

The following facts and concerns were taken into account in arriving at our conclusions:
For more than a century, vaccinations have been an essential public health tool in preventing the
spread of a growing number of infectious and preventable diseases, including small pox, polio, measles,
influenza and, most recently, Covid-19.
The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) is a federal committee within the
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) that provides evidence-based recommendations for
vaccine use to control preventable diseases in the U.S.
ACIP’s recommendations typically become official CDC policy and the standard of care, and health
insurance companies and government programs like Medicaid and Medicare are, with few exceptions,
required to cover the vaccinations ACIP recommends at no cost to the patient.
In June 2025, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.,
fired all members of the ACIP and later replaced them with other physicians and researchers, many of
whom have expressed skepticism about vaccines or vaccine mandates.
In August 2025, Kennedy fired CDC director Susan Monarez; other top CDC officials resigned in
protest, including Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, director of the CDC’s National Center for Immunization and
Respiratory Diseases. Monarez later told Congress that she had been fired because she refused to pre-
approve planned ACIP changes in childhood vaccine schedules.
At its annual meeting in September 2025, the newly constituted ACIP voted to recommend, for
the first time, that patients speak with a clinician about the risks and benefits of the Covid-19 vaccine.
This vote means that the federal government no longer routinely recommends Covid-19 vaccines,
placing in doubt their availability and coverage by private and public insurance.
On September 5, 2025, New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed an Executive Order allowing
pharmacists to administer Covid-19 vaccines, affording access for all New Yorkers who wish to be
vaccinated. “The Executive Order will be in place for at least 30 days while a long-term legislative solution
is developed to address access to all vaccines in order to combat the Trump Administration’s misguided
attack on immunization and healthcare,” the governor’s office said.
Identical bills introduced in the New York State legislature, S7823A and A8383, sponsored by Sen.
Brad Hoylman-Sigal and Assembly member Micah Lasher, respectively, authorize the State Department
of Health to serve as an alternative source of authority to the federal CDC with regard to vaccine
schedules, to ensure that the accessibility of vaccines in New York is no longer tied to federal regulatory
uncertainty and decision-making by a federal administration.

There are many possible uses of curbside space in our district.

streets safer by forcing drivers to be more cautious. CB7 has asked that the unique traffic calming
treatments employed on West 94th Street between Amsterdam and Central Park West be
replicated on other crosstown streets.

to both cyclists and pedestrians since their first introduction in New York City in 2007. CB7 has
voted for protected bike lanes on numerous avenues and cross streets.

Community Board 7/Manhattan calls on the city’s Department of Transportation to prioritize
safety.

Re: 165 West 86th Street, West Park Presbyterian Church (Amsterdam). Application to the
Landmarks Preservation Commission to demolish the building, pursuant to Section 25-
309(b)(2), on the grounds of hardship.
Full Board Vote: 19 In Favor 10 Against 2 Abstentions 0 Present
Committee:5-2-0-0. Non-Committee Board Members: 2-1-1-0.
This resolution is based on the following facts and circumstances:
The subject building (the “Church Building”) is a landmark church building constructed ca.
1889- 90 in the Romanesque Revival style designed by Henry Kilburn, an architect, who modified
and re-clad an earlier chapel designed by Leopold Eidlitz in the Victorian-Gothic style. It was
designated an individual landmark in 2010. The Church Building is situated at the Northeast
corner of Amsterdam Avenue and West 86th Street in Manhattan and features two primary
facades – one facing Amsterdam Avenue, and one facing West 86th Street. The primary facades
are constructed of two types of red sandstone. The secondary facades are largely composed of
common brick. The primary facades consist of alternating gabled sections, square towers, and
recessed planes, topped by a series of broadly sloping, pyramidal, or bell-shaped roofs. They
include subtly decorated recessed lancet and round stained-glass windows among other
significant architectural features. The West 86th Street façade includes a separate but integrated
structure containing offices, classrooms and other community spaces (the “Community House”).
According to the January 12, 2010 Landmarks Preservation Commission’s Designation Report
(No. 425 LP-2338), “the West Park Presbyterian Church is considered to be one of the best
examples of a Romanesque Revival religious structure in New York City” and “is one of the Upper
West Side’s most important buildings.” Over the years the congregation has been a center of
activism with the Church Building hosting Chinese congregants in the 19th century, leading on
Civil Rights and anti-Vietnam War activism in the 1960s and 1970s, and hosting the founding
location of West Side Food Pantry and God’s Love We Deliver.
The proposed application is for the granting of a hardship which would allow non-
appropriate work to be done on the landmarked building—in this case the demolition of the
building. The application is based on the claim that the present condition of the Church Building
is profoundly deteriorated and is unsafe; that the cost to renovate, repair and restore the Church
Building is significantly beyond the ability of the Church and the Presbytery to which it belongs
to fund or raise; that if the necessary funds were invested in the Church Building, it would not be
possible to earn the statutorily acceptable rate of return on such an investment; and that
pursuant to a contract entered into between the Church and Presbytery with Alchemy Properties,
a development partner, a new as-of-right mixed residential and commercial building would be
built on the site (conditioned upon demolition) that would include 10,000 square feet of space

designated an individual landmark in 2010. The Church Building is situated at the Northeast
corner of Amsterdam Avenue and West 86th Street in Manhattan and features two primary
facades – one facing Amsterdam Avenue, and one facing West 86th Street. The primary facades
are constructed of two types of red sandstone. The secondary facades are largely composed of
common brick. The primary facades consist of alternating gabled sections, square towers, and
recessed planes, topped by a series of broadly sloping, pyramidal, or bell-shaped roofs. They
include subtly decorated recessed lancet and round stained-glass windows among other
significant architectural features. The West 86th Street façade includes a separate but integrated
structure containing offices, classrooms and other community spaces (the “Community House”).

(No. 425 LP-2338), “the West Park Presbyterian Church is considered to be one of the best
examples of a Romanesque Revival religious structure in New York City” and “is one of the Upper

activism with the Church Building hosting Chinese congregants in the 19th century, leading on
Civil Rights and anti-Vietnam War activism in the 1960s and 1970s, and hosting the founding
location of West Side Food Pantry and God’s Love We Deliver.

This resolution is based on the following facts and circumstances:
The subject building (the “Church Building”) is a landmark church building constructed ca.
1889- 90 in the Romanesque Revival style designed by Henry Kilburn, an architect, who modified
and re-clad an earlier chapel designed by Leopold Eidlitz in the Victorian-Gothic style. It was
designated an individual landmark in 2010. The Church Building is situated at the Northeast
corner of Amsterdam Avenue and West 86th Street in Manhattan and features two primary
facades – one facing Amsterdam Avenue, and one facing West 86th Street. The primary facades
are constructed of two types of red sandstone. The secondary facades are largely composed of
common brick. The primary facades consist of alternating gabled sections, square towers, and
recessed planes, topped by a series of broadly sloping, pyramidal, or bell-shaped roofs. They
include subtly decorated recessed lancet and round stained-glass windows among other
significant architectural features. The West 86th Street façade includes a separate but integrated
structure containing offices, classrooms and other community spaces (the “Community House”).
According to the January 12, 2010 Landmarks Preservation Commission’s Designation Report
(No. 425 LP-2338), “the West Park Presbyterian Church is considered to be one of the best
examples of a Romanesque Revival religious structure in New York City” and “is one of the Upper
West Side’s most important buildings.” Over the years the congregation has been a center of
activism with the Church Building hosting Chinese congregants in the 19th century, leading on
Civil Rights and anti-Vietnam War activism in the 1960s and 1970s, and hosting the founding
location of West Side Food Pantry and God’s Love We Deliver.
The proposed application is for the granting of a hardship which would allow non-
appropriate work to be done on the landmarked building—in this case the demolition of the
building. The application is based on the claim that the present condition of the Church Building
is profoundly deteriorated and is unsafe; that the cost to renovate, repair and restore the Church
Building is significantly beyond the ability of the Church and the Presbytery to which it belongs
to fund or raise; that if the necessary funds were invested in the Church Building, it would not be
possible to earn the statutorily acceptable rate of return on such an investment; and that
pursuant to a contract entered into between the Church and Presbytery with Alchemy Properties,
a development partner, a new as-of-right mixed residential and commercial building would be
built on the site (conditioned upon demolition) that would include 10,000 square feet of space

recessed planes, topped by a series of broadly sloping, pyramidal, or bell-shaped roofs. They

Full Board Vote: 41 In Favor 0 Against 1 Abstention 0 Present
Committee: 9-0-1-0.
The following facts and concerns were taken into account in arriving at our conclusions:
● The Columbus Avenue curb in front of Trader Joe’s at 93rd Street currently allows parking for any vehicle
with a commercial license plate.
● This means that curbside parking is often unavailable to the many trucks delivering goods to Trader
Joe’s, requiring the trucks to double-park in a travel lane of Columbus Avenue, reducing this major
southbound avenue and truck route to two lanes.
● Due to the lack of curbside space, Trader Joe’s employees often temporarily store pallets of goods on
the 20-foot-wide sidewalk outside the store’s storage entrance.
● A dedicated truck loading zone would increase the likelihood that trucks supplying Trader Joe’s will be
able to park at the curb
● The loading zone will be long enough to allow pallets of goods to be temporarily stored at the curb
rather than on the sidewalk.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan approves the installation of a
dedicated truck loading zone at the southwest corner of Columbus Avenue and West 93rd Street for 670
Columbus Avenue, d/b/a Trader Joe’s, consistent with the 100-foot design presented at CB7’s December 2025
Transportation Committee meeting; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT between the hours of 9:00 PM and 4:00 AM, Trader Joe’s shall not use
the designated loading zone or sidewalk for storage, loading, or unloading activities; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan reminds Trader Joe’s that it should not
obstruct the sidewalk or store any equipment, merchandise, or other material on the sidewalk overnight, and
that Community Board 7/Manhattan calls upon the relevant City agencies to ensure that Trader Joe’s follows
all applicable rules and regulations.

Re: Request by Belnord Retail LLC to DOT to relocate the Citi Bike Station (Site ID 7458.03) located on the south

Full Board Vote: 32 In Favor 6 Against 1 Abstentions 2 Present
Committee: 9-1-0-0.
The following facts and concerns were taken into account in arriving at our conclusions:
● A truck loading zone is needed to accommodate deliveries for a future grocery store tenant at 2372
Broadway.
● Deliveries will involve various vehicle types, including single-unit trucks and WB-50 tractor-trailers.
Approximately 15 deliveries are expected per day, at various times. The prospective tenant participates in
the NYC DOT Off-Hour Delivery (OHD) Program.
● Curbside parking on Amsterdam Avenue is limited and located farther from the loading bay at 2372
Broadway. In addition, a dedicated left-turn lane from Amsterdam Avenue to West 87th Street restricts
available curb space for a truck loading zone, and unloading would have to traverse the protected bike lane.
● Preventing trucks from double-parking or blocking the Amsterdam Avenue bike lane is a priority, as such
obstructions create safety concerns.
● Supporting active ground-floor retail is important to the neighborhood. Adding a loading zone will help
attract and retain commercial tenants and reduce the likelihood of long-term vacant storefronts.
● CB7 seeks to maintain and encourage sustainable transportation options, including biking. This Citi Bike
station sees an average of 170 uses per day and is an important part of neighborhood micro mobility
infrastructure. Any relocation should keep the station close to its current position so that regular users can
continue to rely on it.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT to accommodate a new 65-foot truck loading zone at this location,
Community Board 7/Manhattan approves the relocation of the Citi Bike station (Site ID 7458.03), currently located
on the south side of West 87th Street between Broadway and Amsterdam Avenue, to an alternative site for the Citi
Bike station, which the New York City Department of Transportation will select following further input and analysis
on potential alternative locations within vicinity of the original site; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT the removal of the current Citi Bike station and the installation of the
loading zone are contingent upon the New York City Department of Transportation presenting a satisfactory
proposal for an appropriately located replacement station as close to the current station as possible. The Board
requests that NYC DOT analyze suitable nearby sites, ideally within one block of the existing station, with a strong
preference for a site on the same block, and return to the committee with proposed locations. The DOT must return
to seek approval of the creation of a loading zone, hours of operation of the loading zone, and location of the
loading zone.

Re: River Run Playground Reconstruction Resolution
Full Board Vote: 41 In Favor 0 Against 0 Abstentions 0 Present
Committee: 8-0-0-0.
The following facts and concerns were considered in arriving at our conclusion:
River Run Playground (“the Playground”) is located in Riverside Park at West 82nd Street. Its existing
features include swings, seesaws, play structures for multiple age groups, spray elements, a sandbox designed by
local artist Gerry Augustine Lynas, and the Playground’s distinctive runnel water feature (the river). Although
well-loved, the Playground is worn and outdated and affected by drainage, accessibility, and infrastructure
challenges.
On August 27, 2025, the NYC Department of Parks and Recreation (“DPR”) presented an initial plan (“Initial
Plan”) for reconstruction that reflected priorities informed in part by DPR’s community outreach. The Committee
approved the Initial Plan but noted during the committee meeting that the removal of the existing runnel water
feature would likely be a concern for the community.
Following that meeting, community feedback expressed deep dissatisfaction with several aspects of the
Initial Plan, particularly the removal of the runnel. In response, DPR prepared a revised design (“Revised Plan”) that
restores the runnel and improves upon several elements of the Initial Plan. On December 15, 2025, DPR presented
the Revised Plan (the “Reconstruction”) to the Committee. Major updates include:
● Restored runnel water feature, using more durable materials and an improved layout.
● Expanded plantings and enhanced tree protection, including enlarged tree pits and new native plantings
● Improved accessibility, including accessible play equipment, clear circulation paths, seating, and new
ADA-compliant ramps.
● Enhanced drainage and permeability to reduce flooding and improve site conditions.
● Updated play equipment and spaces, including revised play structures, water play features, a new four-seat
seesaw, improved surfacing, fencing, seating, and bottle-filling stations.
Having reviewed the substantial revisions made in direct response to community concerns, including the
restoration of the runnel, along with improvements to planting conditions, accessibility, drainage, and playground
spaces,
BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan enthusiastically approves the Revised Plan for the
Reconstruction of River Run Playground.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan sincerely thanks NYC Parks for their
responsiveness to constituent feedback and for their willingness to revisit and refine the design in order to meet
community priorities.
Community Board 7 / Manhattan

Date: February 3, 2026
Committee of Origin: Transportation
Re: Improving Compliance with Street Sweeping Regulations
Full Board Vote: 29 In Favor 9 Against 1 Abstention 0 Present
Committee: 10-1-0-0.
The following facts and observations were taken into consideration in reaching our conclusions:
a. Community Board 7/ Manhattan(MCB7) conducted a ride-along with a Department of Sanitation (DSNY)
mechanical street sweeper on the Upper West Side, which documented significant challenges to effective
street cleaning; and
b. CB7 observed numerous instances of cars blocking the street sweeper or drivers refusing to move out of its
way, repeatedly impeding its path and preventing thorough cleaning of curb lanes; and
c. DSNY workers experienced frequent verbal harassment and aggressive behavior from drivers, creating unsafe
working conditions and further slowing operations; and
d. Current enforcement mechanisms are limited and inconsistent, requiring in-person enforcement that is often
impractical while street sweepers are in motion; and
e. Blocked street sweepers reduce street cleanliness, contribute to debris accumulation in gutters and catch
basins, and undermine the City’s investment in sanitation services; and
f. Automated enforcement tools have been shown to improve compliance and reduce conflicts between City
workers and motorists; and
g. The fine for blocking street sweepers in our district is $65, with no increased fine for repeat offenses; and
h. The mid-range price of a monthly space in a parking garage in our district ranges from $500 to more than $800
a month, according to ParkWhiz; and
i. More than one-third of all parking tickets the city gave drivers for blocking street sweepers during a recent
two-year period went to motorists who had already gotten fined for the same offense half a dozen times or
more; and
j. Drivers waiting for the street sweeper typically run their engines, in violation of New York City’s idling laws.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan supports the reintroduction of Int. 0764-2024
in the 2026 City Council legislative session, or similar legislation to authorize the use of enforcement cameras on DSNY
street sweepers to ticket vehicles that block or obstruct street cleaning operations because they are unattended or
because their drivers refuse to move; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT the City increase fines for blocking street sweepers, with substantially higher
penalties for repeat violations; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT the City Council restart the DSNY’s program of placing large, brightly colored
stickers non-obstructively on the windshields of cars violating Alternate-Side Parking rules, a practice banned by the
Council in 2012; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan calls on the relevant City agencies to strictly
enforce existing idling and traffic laws during street sweeping operations.
Community Board 7 / Manhattan

Date: February 3, 2026
Committee of Origin: Youth, Education & Libraries
Re: Support for ensuring functioning air conditioning and repair of mechanical systems at building M118 (154 West 93rd
Street).
Full Board Vote: 41 In Favor 0 Against 0 Abstentions 0 Present
Committee: 7-0-0-0.
The following facts and circumstances were considered by the Committee:
• Building M118 at 154 West 93 Street houses multiple District 3 schools with diverse academic and mandated
instructional needs and relies heavily on stable indoor climate conditions to support learning and operations.
• Internal reporting suggests that all classrooms have functioning air conditioning. However, school administration
and PA/PTA leaders report that this is not accurate, identifying numerous rooms that are unable to maintain safe
temperatures or rely on units that do not function reliably.
• The Building Condition Assessment Survey for 2024 to 2025 identifies significant deficiencies in climate control
systems within M118 which contradict the assertion that cooling systems are fully functional, including:
o defective DX split system indoor units
o fifty five defective temperature control thermostats
o sixty defective terminal unit control valves
o a building wide pneumatic control system operating at zero to twenty percent capacity and rated between
fair and poor
o defective damper actuators affecting airflow to major areas including the cafeteria and gym
o additional ventilation, exhaust, and mechanical issues affecting climate stability
• Shared instructional spaces within M118 including the gymnasium, cafeteria, auditorium, and multipurpose rooms
lack functioning air conditioning or ventilation systems sufficient to support required physical education,
mandated services, state testing, assemblies, and academic programming.
• The combined findings from school leadership and the Building Condition Assessment Survey demonstrate that
M118 requires climate control improvements to ensure safe, equitable, and instructionally sound environments.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT the Youth Education and Libraries (YEL) Committee of Community Board 7/
Manhattan (MCB7) calls for an updated and independently verified evaluation of all classroom air conditioning units and
mechanical systems at M118 to correct discrepancies between reporting and actual building conditions.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT MCB7 supports the installation, repair, and maintenance of functioning air
conditioning in all classrooms located within M118, including necessary electrical or mechanical upgrades.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT MCB7 supports the installation of functioning air conditioning in all shared
instructional spaces within M118 including the gymnasium, cafeteria, auditorium, and multipurpose rooms used for core
instruction, mandated services, or large group programming.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT MCB7 urges the New York City Council, the Manhattan Borough Presidents Office,
the Department of Education, and the School Construction Authority to prioritize capital funding for M118 through Reso
A, Participatory Budgeting, capital planning, and other relevant sources.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT MCB7 will continue monitoring M118 climate control issues, engaging with school
administration and PA/PTA leaders, and incorporating these needs into future District Statements of Needs and Board
advocacy.
Community Board 7 / Manhattan

Date: February 3, 2026
Committee of Origin: Youth, Education & Libraries
Re: Support for ensuring functioning air conditioning in all classrooms and shared instructional spaces in District 3
schools within MCB7 boundaries.
Full Board Vote: 41 In Favor 0 Against 0 Abstentions 0 Present
Committee: 7-0-0-0.
The following facts and circumstances were considered by the Committee:
1. Schools within Community Board 7/ Manhattan (MCB7) boundaries serve thousands of District 3 students across
varying instructional, social, emotional, and mandated service needs, all of which require safe and consistent
learning environments.
2. Many schools report excessive heat in classrooms and shared instructional spaces, resulting in disrupted teaching,
compromised testing conditions, and negative effects on student health, concentration, and staff working
conditions.
3. While the Department of Education and School Construction Authority internal reporting often indicates that all
classrooms have functioning air conditioning, ongoing feedback from school administration and PAPTA leaders
indicates that many units do not function properly, do not cool adequately, or cannot maintain safe temperatures
throughout the instructional day.
4. Shared instructional spaces including gymnasiums, cafeterias, auditoriums, multipurpose rooms, and resource
rooms play a critical role in daily instruction and mandated services but are frequently not equipped with
functioning air conditioning, limiting their instructional usability.
5. Ensuring functioning climate control in both classrooms and shared spaces aligns with priorities related to
instructional equity, student and staff well-being, mandated services, testing requirements, and safe learning
environments.
6. Schools across the district have expressed the need for coordinated capital support, electrical upgrades,
mechanical improvements, and more accurate building-level assessments that reflect real on-site conditions.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7 / Manhattan (MCB7) calls for updated, transparent, and
independently verified assessments of classroom air conditioning units and building climate control systems for all schools
located within MCB7 boundaries.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT MCB7 supports the installation, repair, and maintenance of functioning air
conditioning in all classrooms across District 3 schools within the Board boundaries, including all necessary electrical or
mechanical upgrades.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT MCB7 supports the installation and maintenance of functioning air conditioning
in all shared instructional spaces including gymnasiums, cafeterias, auditoriums, multipurpose rooms, and any space used
for mandated services, testing, assemblies, or academic programming.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT MCB7 urges the New York City Council, Manhattan Borough Presidents Office,
the Department of Education, and the School Construction Authority to prioritize District 3 climate control needs through
Reso A capital allocations, Participatory Budgeting, capital planning, and all available funding avenues.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT MCB7 affirms its commitment to collaborating with school administration and
PAPTA leaders to ensure that functioning air conditioning remains a priority in future District Statements of Needs and
Board advocacy.
Community Board 7 / Manhattan

The following informs the need for condemnation and the action that is needed to be taken to counter the
hateful rise in anti-Semitism:
The safety, dignity, and civil rights of all residents and visitors in New York City are fundamental to the
health and well-being of the City’s diverse communities;
According to official statistics from the New York City Police Department (NYPD), there were 31
reported antisemitic incidents in January 2026—representing a disturbing pattern of bias-motivated conduct
directed against Jewish New Yorkers;
Antisemitic incidents in New York City have constituted a significant share of reported hate crimes,
creating fear and insecurity within Jewish communities and undermining the core values of mutual respect,
inclusion, and public safety;
Prejudice, discrimination, and hate-motivated conduct in any form—against any race, religion, ethnicity,
or identity—are antithetical to the principles of equality, justice, and human dignity;
Combating antisemitism and all forms of hate requires both moral condemnation and concrete action
from government bodies, law enforcement, educators, and community leaders; and
New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin has announced a comprehensive Five-Point Action Plan to
Combat Antisemitism that proposes concrete measures to strengthen protections, expand education, improve
reporting and data, and support community safety in response to rising antisemitism in the city.
Speaker Menin’s Five-Point Action Plan includes the following elements with the exception of item 2 in Speaker
Menin plan:
1. Major Investment in Holocaust Education and Legislation on Discriminatory Misinformation—
Providing new funding for the Museum of Jewish Heritage A Living Memorial to the Holocaust, and
advancing educational initiatives, including materials for students on how social media can contribute
to antisemitism and other forms of hate.
2. Private School Security Infrastructure Reimbursement Program—Creating a needs-based program to
assist private and religious schools in installing security infrastructure such as cameras.

The following facts were taken into consideration:
● NYCHA formally announced on December 23, 2025 that nine developments in Community District 7 will
enter the PACT/RAD program through the following press release: NYCHA Builds on Momentum of the
PACT Program with Request for Expressions of Interest Soliciting Partners for 27 Developments Across
New York City. (NYCHA RFEI (Request for Expressions of Interest) for PACT Citywide Clusters)
o “PACT (Permanent Affordability Commitment Together) is a NYCHA Program through which
developments selected to be a part of the program will receive comprehensive renovations,
enhanced property management, and expanded on-site social services. Through PACT,
developments will be included in the federal Rental Assistance Demonstration (RAD) [plan] and
convert to a more stable, federally-funded program called Project-Based Section 8. This allows
NYCHA to unlock funding to complete comprehensive repairs, while also ensuring homes remain
permanently affordable and residents have the same basic rights as they possess in the public
housing program.” 1
o NYCHA Permanent Affordability Commitment Together (PACT) Resources for Residents
o PACT Program Briefing: Upper West Side Developments (Presentation by NYCHA, October 17,
2025)
● Here is a map of all of the NYCHA Developments in Community District 7, including nine developments
that are starting the RAD/PACT conversion process now.
● MCB7 has received significant feedback from NYCHA residents and community stakeholders voicing
concerns about the conversion, and received requests to assist the tenants in how best to protect their
rights through the shift from the current Section 9 Program to the Section 8 Project-Based Program.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan urges the formation of a Public Housing
Task Force to address pressing issues that impact the residents of public housing, particularly the imminent
PACT/RAD conversion of many developments in Community District 7.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT this Public Housing/NYCHA Task Force shall meet regularly at least once
a month, or as needed, and shall be composed of public housing resident leaders, community board members,
representatives of elected officials, community partners, and representatives from NYC Agencies (e.g., NYCHA,
NYPD, DOB, HUD), as needed. The work of the Task Force, along with any additional information provided by

The Task Force shall ensure transparent communication, and foster positive relationships between
NYCHA and the resident leaders during the imminent PACT/RAD conversion of the designated sites in our
district. In addition, this group will serve as a platform for resident leaders to voice their concerns, to offer input,
and to stay informed about any pending issues, timelines, that will impact the daily lives of public housing
residents who reside in all of the public housing complexes in our district. The key objectives shall be:
● Communication & Transparency: Provide regular updates on any changes that may affect residents
of the public housing community.
● Open Meetings Law: In accordance with the Open Meetings Law requirements, the Task Force’s
meetings shall be public when a quorum of the Task Force is present. Specifically, the following shall
be provided:
a. Task Force meetings shall be properly noticed on the MCB7 website. The public shall have
the right to attend all such meetings.
b. The monthly and as needed meetings shall be recorded and the recording shall be posted
to Youtube.
● Impact Mitigation: Identify and address potential challenges related to health, safety and disruptions
to the daily lives of residents.
● Safety & Environmental Concerns: Ensure compliance of safety policies and standards.
● Community Engagement: Foster open dialogue between resident leaders and NYCHA management
and administrators allowing residents to raise concerns quickly and share suggestions for
improvement.
● Advocacy & Accountability: Advocate on behalf of the resident leaders’ interests to ensure that
commitments made by NYCHA are upheld and that any issues are addressed promptly.
● Future Scope of Work: Determine the continuing scope of work for the Task Force that will address
the resident leaders’ concerns and the ongoing work at all of the NYCHA developments in Community
District 7.

Re: Housing & Land Use project proposed for MCB7 Funding- SRO Housing Survey and Strategy
Full Board Vote: 34 In Favor 1 Against 0 Abstentions 0 Present
Committee: 13-0-0-0.
The following facts were taken into consideration:
● Single-room occupancy (SRO) housing was historically a vital component of the rental market on
the Upper West Side (CD7) and across New York City, providing essential low-income housing.
● The dramatic decline of SRO units, now constituting less than one percent of the City’s rental stock,
has significantly contributed to the ongoing housing crisis and the rise in homelessness.
● Manhattan Community Board 7 (MCB7) had identified the need for a 2025/2026 Planning Fellow to
conduct a comprehensive study to address this decimation through updated data and policy
recommendation, and submitted an unsuccessful application to the Fund for the City of New York.
Please see HERE for that application.
● The proposed project would deliver a detailed survey, map, and database of the current SRO
inventory in CD7, building upon previous studies conducted by MCB7 over the last 15 years.
● The project aims to identify current regulatory impediments to new SRO development and create a
strategy to preserve existing units from being converted to higher-profit uses. The final deliverables
will include an outreach plan to arm local and state elected officials with the data and roadmap
necessary to legalize and encourage the expansion of SRO housing.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board / Manhattan supports the application for
community board funding for this project to ensure the preservation and expansion of this critical housing
type in our community.
Community Board 7 / Manhattan

should have adequate financial recourse for injuries sustained in such an accident. One resolution called for
registration of Class 2 and Class 3 e-bikes, e-scooters ,insurance, helmet use and enhanced enforcement of traffic

outnumber any other category and, in a recent MCB7 Public Safety Survey inquiring as to which actions would
most improve safety in our community, E-bike traffic enforcement was the #1 response.
• Despite these concerns, no legislation, on the State or City level enacting the above requirements has been passed
to date. Various bills are currently stalled in committee in both of those legislative bodies. This failure to act has
resulted in virtually non-existent enforcement of Vehicle and Traffic Law violations, largely because there is no
means of identification of violators, as well as a lack of recourse for accident victims.

pedestrians, have grown as well.

registration and insurance for their deliverers.

electric assisted bicycles and scooters,registration, including the issuance of readily visible license plates, maintaining

Vote: In Favor Against Abstention Present
Re: Rent Regulations.
PREAMBLE
Rent regulations for rent regulated apartments in New York City are
authorized by a grant of state authority to the city council (and to other
local governments through-out the state for their areas). The local
government is limited in that it cannot establish a regulation that is "more
onerous on the landlord" (taken from the State Law) than the state's
regulation, but it can enact locally less protective regulations, or no
regulations at all. In 1994, for example, the City Council introduced a
version of "luxury decontrol" that was then expanded upon by the state
government in 1997, resulting in (1) average rental prices for new leases in
CB 7 that are significantly above the average monthly income for families in
this area, and (2) a large decrease in the number of Rent Regulated family
apartments. Since 1995, these luxury decontrol provisions have been
combined with a policy change in the treatment of capital improvement
"pass alongs" with the effect, in higher rent neighborhoods like CB7, of
establishing de facto vacancy decontrol of rental apartments.
More than seventy-four percent of the residents of CB7 are renters, most of
these under some form of rent (protection) regulation. For those protected
by rent regulations, families of moderate means and seniors and the
disabled, especially, the continuation of rent regulations is critical to their
well-being, and something they demand of their government. In the year
2000, the New York City rent regulations expire, and the City Council must
act to renew them. Because of term limits, most members of the current city
council will be leaving their positions at the end of 2000 and most will be
seeking new elected positions. The Real Estate Industry is the number one
contributor to local campaigns, for both political parties, in New York State.
It has vowed to destroy the rent protections so vital to many in our
community. We fully expect another piece of legislation will attempted to
eliminate or weaken the protections. Many of those who have rented
apartments without protections, moving in to decontrolled units and those
whose apartments have been decontrolled while living in them, are finding
that they cannot afford their apartments at the time of lease renewal. Rents
in parts of our district have increased three to five times in the past five
years. These out of control rent increases are destabilizing our community,
preventing people from establishing roots by limiting their tenure in the
community to the term of their lease. There are currently no new family
apartments that fall under rent protections with exception of those obtained
by developers in barter for tax breaks.
BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan supports the re-
enactment of
rent controls, and the following changes (not withstanding provisions of the
state law to the contrary.)
· Limits luxury decontrol proceedings to tenants under the age of 62, and to
tenants who are not disabled, as defined by the NY City Human Resources
Administration.
· Limits the luxury decontrol of an apartment to the tenant in possession;
succeeding tenants must be offered the apartment at the last controlled
rent plus any legal increment.
· Landlord waives right to luxury decontrol where landlord knowingly rented
apartment to tenant whose income was above threshold for decontrol.
· Increases threshold of luxury decontrol by 25 percent, to reflect inflation
since the time of the initial setting of the threshold.
· Returns to the previous policy that MCI increases are not granted for
vacant apartments, and that rent increases cannot exceed a combined 20
percent per year.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan requests
studies
of the following:
· The impact of decontrol on availability of housing in Community District 7
for families whose incomes reflect the diverse range of incomes present in
the district;
· The impact of decontrol on city's real estate tax revenues from this
district;
· The use of MCI and hardship increases and exactly what effect they have
had on current rents;
· Community District 7 as a model for what is likely to happen in other
communities that are hit with either de facto or real decontrol; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan strongly
opposes any weakening of the rent protections, and calls for stronger
enforcement and penalties for those who do not respect these laws (both
landlords and tenants).
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan asks that
the City
Council acts in the best interests of the residents of the City of New York.

Date: March 2, 2000
Committee of Origin: Youth
Full Board Vote: 19 In Favor 0 Against 0 Abstentions 0 Present
Re: NYC budget cuts in Summer Youth Employment Program (SYEP).
WHEREAS, the 1998 federal Workforce Investment Act ("WIA") has
replaced the Summer Youth Employment Program with legislation that
identified summer jobs as one of 10 youth employment activities that
should be offered by cities and states, and does not require that as many
jobs be provided as in the past; and
WHEREAS, the WIA requires the city to provide a broader range of services
to youth participating in the summer jobs program and requires that the city
allocate a minimum of 30% of its WIA youth funds to services for out-of-
school youth up to age 21, resulting in broader services for a larger
population and decreasing substantially the funding available for summer
youth employment opportunities; and
WHEREAS, the values of and need for comprehensive year-round services
for both in-school and out-of-school youth is evident; and
WHEREAS, the loss of thousands of summer jobs will impact tremendously
the city's youth, families and communities;
BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan requests that:
q City officials maximize the use of federal dollars to support summer jobs;
and
q The city and state make funds available to fill the remaining gap in order
to assure that the number of summer youth jobs opportunities for youth is
at least the same number as were available in 1998 and 1999.

Date: March 2, 2000
Committee of Origin: Youth
Full Board Vote: 19 In Favor 0 Against 0 Abstentions 0 Present
Re: NYC budget cuts in Summer Youth Employment Program (SYEP).
WHEREAS, the 1998 federal Workforce Investment Act ("WIA") has
replaced the Summer Youth Employment Program with legislation that
identified summer jobs as one of 10 youth employment activities that
should be offered by cities and states, and does not require that as many
jobs be provided as in the past; and
WHEREAS, the WIA requires the city to provide a broader range of services
to youth participating in the summer jobs program and requires that the city
allocate a minimum of 30% of its WIA youth funds to services for out-of-
school youth up to age 21, resulting in broader services for a larger
population and decreasing substantially the funding available for summer
youth employment opportunities; and
WHEREAS, the values of and need for comprehensive year-round services
for both in-school and out-of-school youth is evident; and
WHEREAS, the loss of thousands of summer jobs will impact tremendously
the city's youth, families and communities;
BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan requests that:
q City officials maximize the use of federal dollars to support summer jobs;
and
q The city and state make funds available to fill the remaining gap in order
to assure that the number of summer youth jobs opportunities for youth is
at least the same number as were available in 1998 and 1999.

Re: The Department of Housing Preservation and Development's Asset Sales
Program in CD7.
WHEREAS, many city-owned apartment buildings, operated by the
Department of Housing Preservation and Development ("HPD"), are located
in CD7, and these apartments provide housing for a sig-nificant number of
low and moderate income families; and
WHEREAS, HPD is engaged in a program to sell these buildings to the
tenants or private owners, without any requirement that low and moderate
income families be served in the future; and
WHEREAS, HPD has available programs that would return these buildings to
private hands, but would require that they serve income-qualified renters;
and other alternatives to the dispos-session of the these properties, that
would have positive bene-fits for the CD7 community and for the city appear
not to have been explored; and
WHEREAS, this action by HPD will have a substantial impact on the
character of CD7, and has not been submitted to the Board for review;
BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan requests that HPD's
Asset Sales Program be temporarily halted in the district, and submitted to
the Community Board for its review; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7 requests that HPD not
proceed with the sale of any of the four listed buildings at this time; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7 requests that the City
Council direct HPD to obtain the advice of the Community Board before
proceeding with its projected sales; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7 requests that the city
preserve existing low- and moderate-income housing in our community by
employing Tenant Interim Lease or similar programs, rather than
unrestricted Asset Sales.

Vote: 42 In Favor 0 Against 1 Abstentions 0 Present
Re: Extension of the Senior Citizens Rent Increase Exemption.
WHEREAS, the Senior Citizens Rent Increase Exemption ("SCRIE") protects
seniors on limited incomes from annual and biannual rent increases that are
authorized by current rent regulations, because these increases would be a
substantial hardship and would cause many of these tenants to lose their
homes; and
WHEREAS, current state laws reimburse rental housing owners for the
rental income they lose by the SCRIE program through an off-set of their
property taxes, so that the owners do not suffer a loss from the program;
and
WHEREAS, the SCRIE policy is beneficial to the community because it
tempers the need for higher rents with fairness and justice and prevents
homelessness of seniors who would, in addition to their suffering, become
public burdens; and
WHEREAS, the household income limits for eligibility into the SCRIE
Program is set at $20,000 and this number does not adequately reflect the
current market trend or the changes enacted in the RCRS code allowing for
additional increases not previously proposed or enacted; and
WHEREAS, a number of tenants of Rent Controlled/Rent Stabilized and
Mitchell-Lama apartments are people with permanent disabilities whose
incomes are limited, and often derived solely from governmental programs
such as SSI and SSD; and
WHEREAS, the state contribution to SSI has not increased in ten years, so
that the maximum now provided to an SSI recipient is only $599 per month;
and
WHEREAS, average regulated rents have more than doubled in the past ten
years and now exceed the maximum disability support of a person on SSI;
and
WHEREAS, many of people with disabilities are not eligible for the existing
SCRIE program because they do not meet the minimum age requirement;
and
WHEREAS, many people with disabilities will lose their homes because of
the state authorized increases in regulated rents;
BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7 Manhattan urges the Mayor of
the City of New York, the City Council, and the NY State Legislature to
expand eligibility into the SCRIE program to include people with disabilities
(SSI, SSD), regardless of age, who otherwise meet the requirements of the
SCRIE eligibility; and to increase said household income caps to $25,000
allowing for a more broad and encompassing program further protecting
seniors from excessive increases as the program originally intended.
RESOLUTION
Date: May 2, 2000
Committee of Origin: Landmarks Committee
Full Board

Vote: 27 In Favor 8 Against 2 Abstentions 0 Present
Re: Placement of the Alfred Nobel obelisk at Central Park West and 81st
Street.
WHEREAS, in response to the 81st Street community, the Department of
Parks and Recreation ("DPR"), withdrew its original proposed location for
the placement of the Alfred Nobel monument which was formerly at West
81st Street, west of Central Park West; and
WHEREAS, DPR has thoroughly explored all placement options for the
monument, and believes the chosen location is the best for several reasons;
and
WHEREAS, the new location, approximately 100 feet south of West 81st
Street on the Museum side of Central Park West, abutting Theodore
Roosevelt Park, will make the monument readily accessible to museum-
goers and others; and
WHEREAS, the location is appropriate for several reasons, including that the
American Museum of Natural History is a world-renowned scientific
institution appropriate to such a monument; Theodore Roosevelt was the
first recipient of the Nobel Prize, and Margaret Mead was a recipient as well;
and the monument itself celebrates all the American Nobel Prize laureates
and intellectual, scientific, and literary achievements befitting the
placement near this Museum; and
WHEREAS, the existing fence on Central Park West will be reconfigured into
a semi-circle at this location to surround the sculpture, so that people can
walk around it to read the names of the American recipients of the Nobel
Prizes that are inscribed on all sides without the sculpture impacting either
on the sidewalk space, or on the views of either the Planetarium or the
Theodore Roosevelt Memorial wing of the Museum; nor will it interfere with
the roots of nearby trees;
BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan approves the
proposed location to install the Alfred Nobel monument abutting Theodore
Roosevelt Park, on Central Park West about 100 feet south of West 81st

RESOLUTION
Date: October 3, 2000
Committee of Origin: Housing
Re: NYC Housing Authority's Annual Plan for 2001.
Full Board Vote: 43 In Favor 1 Against 1 Abstention 1 Present
WHEREAS, Community District 7 is home to residents of Douglass Houses
and Addition, Amsterdam Houses and Addition, Wise Towers, De Hostos
Apartments, Dome Apartments, and other New York City Housing Authority
("NYCHA") housing; and
WHEREAS, Community Board 7/Manhattan ("CB7") regularly assists NYCHA
residents and management in resolving housing maintenance, public safety,
quality-of-life and other issues that are brought to the Board’s attention,
and was recently successful in requesting that the City Comptroller audit
the NYCHA repair notification process, thereby exposing serious
management failures that are finally being addressed; and
WHEREAS, CB7 has taken a leadership role in providing information about
new NYCHA housing policies to residents, including sponsoring several well-
attended forums on NYCHA’s Draft 2000 and 2001 Plans; and
WHEREAS, CB7 has reviewed NYCHA’s 2001 Draft Plan ("the Plan") and the
statements of local elected officials who testified at NYCHA’s August 17,
2000 hearing on the Plan; has held a community forum on July 31, 2000,
attended by approximately 200 residents and other members of the
community, at which both governmental and non-governmental experts
reviewed the Plan, and the Board received comments from residents and
resident leaders; and
WHEREAS, CB7 recognizes that NYCHA has made positive changes in the
plan over the past two years during the consultation process, but continues
to be concerned with several aspects of the plan; and
WHEREAS, NYCHA is scheduled to submit its Final Plan to the Department of
Housing and Urban Development on October 14, 2000;
BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan opposes the Plan’s
requirement that public housing residents fulfill eight hours of community
service a month. Mandating that residents serve the community to avoid
eviction is tantamount to forced labor, and is counter-productive because it
diminishes the perceived value of volunteer work. Rather, NYCHA should
encourage volunteer and community-building efforts among all residents,
and provide backup support for their efforts; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7 opposes the Plan's
proposal to “deconcentrate” certain housing developments designated as
low-income. The Plan would offer unspecified incentives to families with
higher incomes to encourage them to move into developments designated
as low-income. Currently, there are about 125,000 families on the waiting
list for public housing, and about 80% of these are lower income. As
vacancies develop, lower income families will be skipped in favor of higher
income families. CB7 believes this policy is unwise and unfair, and the
current first-come, first-served waiting list should be respected. Community
Board 7 calls on NYCHA to develop a balanced plan that fairly distributes
available housing units to all eligible individuals and families.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7 opposes the proposal
to relax eviction procedures thereby altering the current protection of due
process and review in eviction proceedings. Community Board 7 continues
to support the current model which closely resembles existing New York
State tenant protections.

Date: April 3, 2001
Committee of Origin: Health and Human Services Committee
Re: Reducing Pesticide Use and Exposure in New York City.
Full Board

Vote: 32 In Favor 0 Against 0 Abstentions 0 Present
WHEREAS, according to the New York State Department of Environmental
Conservation’s pesticide reporting data for 1997 and 1998, New York City
had the highest use of pesticides in New York State - more than a quarter of
the state's entire pesticide use - even before the West Nile virus spraying
began; and
WHEREAS, the pesticides used most commonly in New York City in 1997 and
1998 were highly toxic insecticides, including substances the U.S.
Environmental Protection Agency subsequently ruled unsafe for use in the
home; and
WHEREAS, pesticides routinely used in New York City have been linked to a
range of acute and chronic health effects, such as asthma and respiratory
illness, neurological damage, cancer, birth defects, endocrine disruption,
and immune system damage; and
WHEREAS, pesticides pose special risks for developing fetuses, infants, and
children, who are exposed to pesticides in their homes, schools, and
playgrounds as well as in their food; and
WHEREAS, safer alternatives exist for preventing and controlling most
urban pest problems, and have been demonstrated to be successful at pilot
projects in New York City, Chicago and Toronto; and
WHEREAS, although local governments in New York are preempted by law
from regulating pesticide use, they may adopt policies to phase out their
own use of hazardous pesticides on municipal property, and local
governments such as Buffalo, Albany, and Westchester County have already
done so; and
WHEREAS, the state of New York recently enacted the Pesticide Neighbor
Notification law, which allows New York City to adopt special requirements
for advance notice to be provided to neighbors before certain lawn pesticide
applications;
BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan calls on City Council
Speaker Peter Vallone, City Council Members Phillip Reed, Bill Perkins and
Ronnie Eldridge, and other members of the New York City Council to enact a
local law to phase out the use of toxic pesticides on city-owned and
operated property, such as public housing, public schools, parks, and
playgrounds, and phase in the use of non-toxic alternatives; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan calls on
City Council Speaker Peter Vallone, City Council Members Phillip Reed, Bill
Perkins and Ronnie Eldridge, and other members of the New York City
Council to provide funding in the 2001-2002 city budget for an independent
evaluation of each City agency’s pesticide use and pest control practices,
including recommendations for nontoxic pest management alternatives; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan calls on
City Council Speaker Peter Vallone, City Council Members Phillip Reed, Bill
Perkins and Ronnie Eldridge, and other members of the New York City
Council to adopt the state’s Pesticide Neighbor Notification Law so that
neighbors can avoid exposure to hazardous lawn care pesticides; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan calls on
Manhattan Borough President C. Virginia Fields to encourage the City
Council to enact a local law to phase out the use of toxic pesticides on city-
owned and operated property, to provide funding in the 2001-2002 city
budget for an independent evaluation of each City agency’s pesticide use
and pest control practices, and to adopt the state’s Pesticide Neighbor
Notification Law; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan calls for
this Resolution to be circulated to Manhattan’s other Community Boards for
their consideration of similar and appropriate action by the City of New York
to reduce community exposure to toxic pesticides.

Vote: 29 In Favor 0 Against 0 Abstention 0 Present
WHEREAS, Community Board 7/Manhattan has long expressed its concern
for homeless individuals residing on city streets and in other public places,
and for the best way to help the street-bound homeless chain shelter and
services; and
WHEREAS, there are many homeless individuals in Community Board
7/Manhatan; and
WHEREAS, ensuring access to emergency shelter for the homeless prevents
the death and injury of street-bound homeless individuals and improves
conditions in city neighborhoods; and
WHEREAS, the Department of Homeless Services has announced plans to
substantially reduce the number of entry points to the emergency shelter
system for homeless single adults; and
WHEREAS, for homeless single men, currently there is only one entry point
to the emergency shelter system citywide (the Vacancy Control Unit, located
at the 30th Street Men's Shelter in Manhattan) and no entry points to the
emergency shelter system in Brooklyn, Queens, or the Bronx; and
WHEREAS, the Department of Homeless Services has announced plans to
create a new non-shelter intake center which would replace the existing
intake center for homeless single men, and would replace the existing entry
points for homeless single women (currently located in three assessment
shelters in Queens the Bronx, and Brooklyn); and
WHEREAS, the current system, with limited entry points to the emergency
shelter system has created barriers to shelter and services for many street-
hound homeless individuals; and
WHEREAS, the record of non-shelter intake centers such as the Bronx
Emergency Assistance Unit (BAU) for homeless families (where the City, in
violation of court order, has forced thousands of children and adults to sleep
over night on floors and benches) and the Vacancy Control Unit for
homeless single men located at the 30th Street Men's Shelter prove that
such non-shelter centers create significant barriers to shelter for homeless
people; and
WHEREAS, most homeless service providers including street outreach
teams, advocate the creation of multiple entry points (including specialized
shelter beds catering to street-bound individuals who are unable initially to
remain at structured programs or large assessment facilities) for the
emergency shelter system, to make it easier for vulnerable street bound
homeless individuals to obtain shelter and services in all of the boroughs;
and
WHEREAS, homeless outreach teams report that the number of homeless
individuals on the streets has risen substantially in recent years, and
currently more than 26.000 homeless men, women and children sleep in the
New York City municipal shelter system each night, representing a
substantial increase from the average daily shelter census of 21,288 in
1998; and
WHEREAS, investments in supportive housing have proven effective in
diminishing homelessness, yet the City's investment in supportive housing
has reduced over the past several years; therefore, be it
RESOLVED, the Department of Homeless Services abandon its plans to
create non-helter intake centers for homeless single adults; and
RESOLVED, the Department of Homeless Services utilize existing shelters to
provide at least one intake shelter for homeless single men and one intake
shelter for homeless single women in Manhattan, Brooklyn the Bronx and
the Queens, respectively: and
RESOLVED, the Department of Homeless Services include low demand
shelter beds in intake shelters to encourage long-term street-bound
homeless individuals to obtain shelter and services; and
RESOLVED, the Department of Homeless Services expand investments in
supportive housing and rental assistance to provide long-term solutions to
the problem of homelessness.

RESOLUTION
Date: October 2, 2001
Committee of Origin: Housing
Re: Platform statement of Housing First!
Full Board

Vote: 33 In favor 4 Against 2 Abstentions 0 Present
WHEREAS, the population of New York City grew over the last decade by
more than 450,000 people to over 8 million while the City constructed only
85,000 new housing units; and
WHEREAS, the City of New York’s capital budget to build and preserve
affordable housing is less than half of what it was in 1990 (adjusted for
inflation); and
WHEREAS, more than 525,000 families at all income levels (one-quarter of
all renter households) pay more than half their income for rent, according to
the U.S. Census Bureau, and 150,000 families live in housing with serious
maintenance or repair problems; and
WHEREAS, the vacancy rate for apartments, at all but the very highest rent
levels, has decreased dramatically over the past four years; it went down by
almost 14 percent for apartments renting under $700 and by 66 percent for
those renting under $400; and
WHEREAS, many housing units built with direct or indirect subsidies are in
jeopardy of being lost to the affordable housing stock; Federal project-
based subsidies, rental restrictions financed with federal Low Income
Housing Tax Credits and the regulatory agreement and long-term tax-
abatements that supported Mitchell-Lama buildings are in the process of
expiring and the inevitable outcome will be that a substantial number of
apartments will be converted to high, market-level rents; and
WHEREAS, the scarcity of affordable housing jeopardizes the City’s
continued economic success as growing companies will be reluctant to
locate or expand here if their employees cannot find affordable places to
live; and
WHEREAS, the crisis affects people at virtually every level of the economic
spectrum: many homeless, low-income, moderate-income, and middle-
income people cannot find decent, affordable housing; and
WHEREAS, the housing crisis undermines quality education and other vital
municipal services; children cannot fulfill their potential in school while
living in overcrowded or substandard housing and teachers and many of the
City’s uniformed service employees who cannot afford to live in New York
City have been forced to find more affordable housing in suburbs far outside
the communities they serve; and
WHEREAS, substandard housing conditions have been linked to chronic
health problems among New Yorkers, especially childhood asthma, further
straining an already overburdened public health care system; and
WHEREAS, New York City has many outstanding housing programs, an
impressive history of public/private partnerships, innovative private
financing approaches, and an infrastructure of not-for-profit and for-profit
developers, but is missing the adequate public investment to meet the
overwhelming housing need;
BE IT RESOLVED THAT the City of New York needs a substantial, multi-year
investment of capital to create new affordable housing and rehabilitate and
preserve the durable housing stock that we have inherited; and
BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan endorses the
platform statement of Housing First! and calls on the City of New York, The
Mayor, Public Advocate, Comptroller, and City Council Members, as well as
the candidates for all these offices, to commit to a ten-year capital
investment of $1 billion per year to create 100,000 new housing units and
rehabilitate and preserve an additional 85,000 housing units.

Date: March 5, 2002
Committee of Origin: Steering
Re: Manhattan Borough President’s proposed term limits for community
board members.
Full Board

Vote: 30 In favor 1 Against 1 Abstention 0 Present
WHEREAS, the Manhattan Borough President has invited response to a
proposal of imposition of term limits for community board members; and
WHEREAS, appointees serve 2-year terms which under current procedures,
the Borough President may reappoint or not at her sole discretion; and
WHEREAS, the Borough President does seek the advice of other elected
officials as well as the current board leadership; and
WHEREAS, community boards may benefit from the historical knowledge and
experience of long serving appointees; and
WHEREAS, term limits would establish an arbitrary condition to service and
deprive the Borough President of the ability to reappoint members on a case by case
basis;
BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan disapproves the
imposition of term limits to community board appointments.
DO NOT USE
WHEREAS,, an option of imposing term limits for appointments to terms of
Community Board members has been made public, be it known that Community
Board 7/Manhattan sees the concept as working against the best capabilities of the
Board.
Currently the process by which Council Members nominate candidates to the
Borough President for two year terms and such appointees must reapply bi-annually
for appointment allows the elected officials to easily limit the time in office of any
non-performing Community Board member, and simultaneously Chairs can bring to
the attention of the Borough President or Council members information about the
clear lack of interest demonstrated by non-participating members so that the effort
to assess performance is of minimal effort.
Long standing members of the Community Board often represent a knowledge
base that can be helpful to newer board members as issues that look to precedents
or history for guidance are to be resolved by the Community Board, they can help
newer members by mentoring efforts and by their demonstrated commitment can
help Board Members engage in serious research on subjects as well as healthy
debate before voting.
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan resolves
that it is not in the best of interest of the local community or the Board's work to
limit terms of Community Board members.

Vote: 21 In favor 2 Against 4 Abstentions 0 Present
WHEREAS, the NYC Department of Public Health has been concerned about
the potential threat posed humans from the spread of West Nile disease by
infected mosquitoes in New York City; and
WHEREAS, the medical and scientific issues posed by this threat, and by the
public health measures to control it, involve technical issues that the
Community Board cannot competently determine; but
WHEREAS, Community Board 7/Manhattan believes that the Department of
Health's attempt to control adult infected mosquitoes in the past two years
by spraying by aircraft, helicopter, or truck on city streets, was ill-
conceived, poorly executed, and unnecessarily exposed large numbers of
people to hazardous agents, producing many reports of asthmatic and other
health-related adverse reactions; and
WHEREAS, the Department of Health has put on staff an experienced
scientist, an entomologist with a specialty in the mosquito and in mosquito
control, and Dr. Markowski has outlined to the Board measured steps,
beginning with bacterial control of mosquito larvae that can be
accomplished with
biological agents that are believed to be innocuous to humans, and with
methods of application that minimize or entirely avoid exposure of the
general population; and
WHEREAS, Dr. Markowski has also stated that if these controls do not
reduce the infected population sufficiently, he may have to recommend
area-wide spraying with an insecticide that will reduce the infected adult
mosquito population;
BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan appreciates the
efforts of the Department of Health to inform the Board of its plans; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7 requests that the
Department of Health make a final determination of its actions only after
consultation with medical and scientific experts, such as the Center for Child
Health and the Environment at the Mount Sinai Medical Center, who assess
the complex public health, individual health, environmental issues; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT if the medical and scientific judgment is
that spraying should be undertaken, that the Department of Health devise a
plan to accomplish this spraying with the least amount of exposure to the
general public possible, and that an energetic multilingual public
information campaign, with specific practical advice on ways to limit
individual exposure, become part of the plan. Community Board 7 also
requests that the Department of Health actively evaluate the campaign for
any adverse effects on individual health through a program of monitoring.
Committee: 6-0-0-0. Board Member: 1-0-0-0.
RESOLUTION
Date: July 2, 2002
Committee of Origin: Health and Human Services
Re: Marriage Equality.
Full Board

Vote: 18 In favor 5 Against 6 Abstentions 0 Present
WHEREAS, same-sex couples are currently denied the option of engaging in
civil marriage in the State of New York; and
WHEREAS, civil marriage confers upon a couple several hundred benefits
and protections under the laws of the State of New York and more than one
thousand benefits and protections under the laws of the government of the
United States; and
WHEREAS, as a result of being denied access to civil marriage, same-sex
couples are denied the numerous benefits and protections afforded through
civil marriage to opposite-sex couples; and
WHEREAS, the Constitution of the Unites States guarantees all citizens
equal protection under the law;
BE RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan calls upon the State of
New York to allow same-sex couples to enter into legally recognized civil
marriages, with all the federal and State benefits and protections that civil
marriage entails; and
BE IT FURHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7 calls upon the State of
New York and the City of New York to recognize the civil marriages of same-
sex couples performed in other states or in foreign countries; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7 calls upon the State of
New York to treat the civil marriage of same-sex couples as identical under
federal and State Law to the civil marriage of an opposite-sex couple; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7 calls upon the City of
New York to treat the civil marriage of same-sex couples as identical under
City Law to the civil marriage of an opposite-sex couple.

question of the disposal of the property, at which hearings many residents

business under the handicap of a month-to-month lease, and that as a

displace individuals and businesses from this community, and that those

Vote: BACK TO COMMITTEE
WHEREAS,, Touro College LLC (i.e. the applicant) proposes to construct a mixed-use building
at 223-227 West 60th Street; and
WHEREAS,, the applicant is requesting six variances from the Board of Standards & Appeals
(BSA) concerning bulk, numbers of dwelling units, and open space requirements;
WHEREAS,, Community Board 7/Manhattan finds that the proposed structure is inappropriate,
overwhelming, and out of scale with the neighborhood; and
WHEREAS,, Community Board 7/Manhattan makes these technical findings in accordance with
Section 72-21 of the Zoning Resolution:
a) The applicant has not demonstrated that there are unique physical conditions peculiar to and inherent in
its zoning lot which conditions prevent the applicant from complying with the Zoning Resolution
b) The applicant’s financial analysis obscures the role of the not-for-profit applicant in the for-profit
development, and Community Board 7/Manhattan is unable to assess its relevance or correctness
regarding reasonable return on investment
c) The applicant has not demonstrated that the application, if granted, will not alter the essential
character of the neighborhood of the street on which the lot is located and will not be detrimental to
the public welfare, and has not demonstrated that the structure for which the variance is being
sought will not substantially impair the appropriate use of the adjacent property
d) Community Board 7/Manhattan is not convinced that the applicant faces difficulties and hardships
necessitating a variance, and so is unable to assess whether any such difficulties or hardships are the
creation of the applicant
e) The applicant has not demonstrated that the application is the minimum variance necessary to
afford the relief the applicant seeks; and
Community Board 7/Manhattan 2
January 2003 Resolutions, continued
WHEREAS,, award of a variance depends on an applicant meeting all five tests of Section 72-21
of the Zoning Resolution; and
WHEREAS,, Community Board 7/Manhattan finds that the applicant has not met findings a), c),
and e);
BE IT RESOLVED THAT Community Board 7/Manhattan disapproves application #315-02-
BZ to the Board of Standards & Appeals (BSA) by Touro College LLC for six variances concerning
bulk, dwelling units, and open space requirements to permit the construction of a mixed-use building at
223-227 West 60th Street (West End –Amsterdam Avenue).
